The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge of California, as follows
BRETHREN OF THE MOST \VORSHIPFUL
GRAND LOOOJ<l DY CALH'ORNIA:
SINCE onr last annual convocation another year has coruc and gone. Jt~ events
are of the past. The hopes it awakened and the sorrows it produced, the joys and
blights it brought, and the tears that it started or dried, are Bwcpt forever from n~.
But we have come together for purposes of the future. It is pleasing to indulge in
retrospects, but only useful as we apply them to the duties and labors of life. Onr
noble Order has a long and glorious history, and it8 unwritten pageo excite the most
glowing memories to which the heart of humanity can cling. Down through the dim
ages its record is as a track of light, where brethren have walked together in safety,
and felt the genial warmth of kinuly sympathies. Its >trong arm of brotherhood lrnF
been a shield to those of the Craft who h:tvc lived before us, and its acliicvcments
have been but ble8sings to our race. As eyery year adds to the history of the Past,
and every event affords a moral, ,;o may onr re!lections 1trni experience, properly ilfl·
plied, open up new channels by which to approach unobtrusively the aboues of want;
and add, without a seeming cause, to the general suru of lrnman lrnppincHB.
Coming together with such Yiews, and animated by the prospects of a glorious
fruition believed to be within the reach of human uchievemcnt, let ns earnestly seek,
as with one heart and purpose, to devise means tltc best calculated to forward the
grand objects of onr Fraternity. I am happy to see among those who have come to
worsliip in the temple of our forefathers, and labor for those wlto are to follow us, the
faces so well remembered in former councils; anti am rejoiced again to grnsp 1iauds
to which fellowship and fidelity have given the mystic assurance that both hunt].~ anti
hearts are those of Masons.
After the vicissitndes and changes of " season, it is fit that we return thanks to
Him who controls the destinies of men and of' all that men devi•e, for the health and
happinesA wl1ich we have enjoyed, arnl for the prcrnperity wliich has atten1led cnu· beloved Order. To His providence we owe onr lives, as well as the mean• of renclering
those Jives useful. By His favor we have been J>rntecte1l from clanger, disease, ancl
death; and are permitted once more to asio\emble in peace 111Hl hrotlierlwod. Onr
grateful acknowledgmentB are justly due, and we shoni<l zeal<msly offer them, for
those blessings so bounteously bestow~d upon ~fasonry and its votaries.
Among the blessings acknowledged, I am iicrmitted to conl(ratnlate you upon the
general exemption of our members from death. But while thi>• is rt wbject of rejoicing, we are yet called upon to sorrow that some l!al'e been sumuioned by the fiat of
our Supreme Ruler to their last account. A few familiar faces nre to be seen no more
on earth. Hearts which have pnlsatecl as warmly as onr own, arc lmshe<l in the eol1! 1uHI
silent grave; hands we have pressed are motionless; and eyes whose exprcssi\'C glcani
of thought and soul were welcomed in fraternal circles, lrnve closed on time and
opened on eternity, We are especially culled to mourn the loss of our wortby brother
O. D. CHAFEE, Grand Tyler of this Grand Lodge, who departed this life on the sixth

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

day of N m·ember last, in his sixty-sixtlr yenr. A long life had heen devoted to the

ARKANSAS.
Our intelligence from the Grand Lodge of this State reaches only to the proceed·
lngs of its Annual Communication commencer! at the city of Little' Hock, on the second day of November, 1857,-the M:. W:. D. P. A11Ms1'RONG, Grancl }faster, p1es'ding,
nucl the R:. W:. Tuos. D. MERRICK being Grauel Secretary.
The Grand Master, in his Acldress, expresses the opinion that the object sought to
be attainecl by the establishment of the system of District Deputy Grand MaHters in
that State, has not been accomplishecl. He deprecates the too frequent change of
officers in the Lodges; recommencls the adoption of a uniform code of by-laws, to be
obligatory upon the subordinates; mentions the appointment of a represent11tive of
the Grand J,ocJge of Ark11nsas near that of Alab11ma ; urges nn interchange of such
representatives with all the Gnmd Lodges ; announces the issue of nine dispensations
to form new Lodges; and strongly advocates the college enterprise several years
1ince begun by the Fraternity in that jurisdiction. In accorclance with a regul11tion
of his Grand Lodge, he presents an abstract of the decisions given by him cluring his
term of office, to none of whiCh clo we see any renson to give dissent, though the
Orancl Loclge adopted the report of a committee expressing opinions arlversc to two
of them. The first, that" a brother who has violnted the law of the land and is in

years, has been advocated by a few of the Grand Lodges of the United States. Our
own views upon this subject have already been presented sufficiently often ; and we
have seen nothil1g thus far to imluce us to change the opimon we have heretofore entertained, that it is an absolute and positive" innovation upon the body of Masonry."
From the remarks presented by Bro. BROWN upon this question, in the earlier portions
of his report, we had supposed that be disagreed with us, toto crew, and was in favor
of the Ohio proposition reqniring a candidate "to express an unqualified belief in the
divine authenticity of the Holy Scriptures"; and certainly the high commendation
and cordial assent which he gives to certain portions of the publications of Delaware,
Mississippi, and Texas, in reference to that subject, might well lead to that supposition. But at a later period we find him using the following language :
"We entirely agree with Bro. MACKEY when he says that' the fundamental law of
Masonry requires only a belief in the Supreme Architect of the Universe.' In our
experience we have never known any other test of faith reqnired of a candidate than
the declaration of a belief and trust in God, because such au assent is an acknowledgment of a belief in the trnth of the revelation by which a knowledge of His existence is obtained, and that implied assent is confirmed by submitting to the ceremonies of initiation. But if we are to understand by this declaration of Bro. MACKRY
that he means t
that a man, who declares his disbelief' in the authenticity of the
Bible, a8 rewrrkd
es and the Prophets, can be made a Mason, then we say we
entirely disagree
im: and, on the other hand, we say with equal assurance, if
the opinions declared by the Grand Lodges of Ohio and Texas,-that 'a distinct
avowal of a belief in the divine authenticity of the Holy Scriptures is an indispensall!e prerequisite to Masonic admii•sion in all Cl1ristian countries,' -is to be understood
as includini; the Goopel of Jesus Ghrist, err the New Testament, then we say we entirely
disagree w1th them, and regard such a 'prerequisite' as a palpable innovation npon
the established landmarks of the Order. '
Now, in all kindness and with sincere respect, we ask our intelligent brother of
Florida if, upon a retrospect of the foregoing paragraph, it will not seem that he
has set up two men of straw for the especial purpose of bringing them both down
with an argumentative brickbat. He perfectly coincides with Bro. MACKEY when he
announces a fundamental law of Masonry which is universally known to tlie intelligent brethren of the Order, and whicl1 is so plain and definite in its language that it
appears scarcely possible that its exact meaning should be involved in any <loubt;
but he "entirely disagrees" with him if that annunciation is intended to me au something which it does not say,-which it can not possibly be construed into,-which
Bro. MAOKEY probably never dreamed of,-and which involves a. negative declaration
of " disbelief" which no Jl.lason perhaps ever heard required of a candidate. On the
other hand, he altogether disagrees with the opinions advanced by the Granu Lodges
of Ohio and Texas, if they are what the word~ in which they are set forth unqualifiedly and unmistakably declare them to be; but, if they are something else, which their
plainly written language renders it impossible to suppose, we are left to infer that he
cordially coincides with them in viewH which as yet they have not presented. After·
all, then, stripped of the supposititious constructions which Bro. BR-OwN's inventive
mind has imagined for the language of thoHe from whom he quotes, his opinion ap·
peartt to be exactly ours- that tJ1e ancient and only religious test 11eretofore known
to Freemasonry should still remain the only one, and that a declaration of' a belief
and trust in God" is all, so far as his religion is concerned, that should be required of

Each of the four Deputy Grand Masters presented Teports at considerable length, and
in the course of them we find the issue of eight other dispensations to establish Lodges. Numerous decisions are recorded, most of which appear to have been governed
by the local law of that jurisdiction. We see no reason to disagree with any of them,
unless perhaps it be with one by Bro. SAMUJn, LAWRIONCE, which declares that" the imposing of flues by a Lodge is not contrary to Masonic law or usage." Though such
action certainly is not opposed to the Masonic law of' England, which he aptly cites in
support of his decision, it as certainly is not in accordance with the general Masonic
u•age of the United States, -the Grand Lodge of Connecticut being the only one we
remember where pecuniary penalties are authorized, and there, we believe, only for
misconduct of the subordinate Lodges.
The Report on Foreign Correspondence, presented by Bro. R. M. SMITH, briefly notices the Communications of' the various American Grand Lodges, but the writer does
not pause to indulge in argument or express opinions. He is kind enough to say of us
that he was" forcibly struck and much pleased with what energy the Grand Secretary
[of' California] had his proceedings published, as they were in the hands of your committee [of' Georgia] in three months after the adjournment of their [our] Communication. How well it would do, and how much pleased we would be to get our own proceedings in so short a time ! " The admiration of our brother will perhaps be increased when we inform him that the proceedings of which he speaks, as well as
those of the year before and after, were on their way to Georgia within thirty clays
after the close of each Communication ; and that six weeks had not elapsed ere the
remotest Lodge in our own State had them in possession. Bro. SMI1'1l says that we
were mistaken in our report of 1857, when we stated that the custom of an Address
from the Grand Master of Georgiu had been abolished. The error, if it were one,
would be unimportant; but, as we have a considerable reverence for facts, and
always read attentively the transactions which we review, in order to present them
with tolerable certainty, we subjoin the following resolution adopted by the Grand
Lodge of Georgia in 1854, and noted by us in our report of 1856 : "Resolved, That the M:. W:. Grand Master appoint, at each meeting of this Grand
Lod"e some member thereof to lecture on the three symbolic degrees of Masonry, in
the pr~sence of said Grand Lodge ; and that said Lecture be in place of the Annual Add1·ess hereafter."
A new Alliman Rezon has been prepared by Grand Master RoCKWEJ,L, for the manuscript of which $2,000 was vote<! to him by the Grand Lodge, and it was ordered to
be published for the use of the Craft in Georgia. The Grand Lodge also presented
him with itH entire librnry, during his life,his own having been destroyed by fire. The
reports relat.ive to the Routhern Masonic Female College, under the patronage of that
body, appear eniiouruging. A Grand Lecturer was ordered to be appointed in each
of the four Masonic DistrictH; and the Grand Secretary reported that no Lodge was
at that date in arrears to the Bran<! Lodge for a single dollar - a statement not a little
creditable to our Georgia brethren. The financial exhibits show a revenue for the
year of $a,832, and an expenditure of $8,572, besides $4,104 invested in a mortgage.
The balance of cash in the treasmy was $1,B62, and the total assets of the Grand
Lodge in caHh, bon<lH, stockH, &c., amonntc<l to $16,217. Two hundred and sixteen
chartered Lodges and one urnler cliHpensation are now borne upon its registry, being
twelve more than were chronicled in mu last report. Three <lays sufficed for the
transaction of its business, and the Grnn<l Master and Grand Secretary were both reelected.

to the general character of Freemasonry. Though we must say that we hardly know
of a case in which a violation of established Masonic usage is not a general matter.
Masonry is one, and no part of the chain can be struck without vibrating in every
link ; and we hold it to be especially the duty of committees on foreign corresponcl·
ence to notice and discuss, boldly but kinclly, everything new that is sought to he in·
troduced. They may be helcl, for instance, to be only local regulations when intro·
duced in a particular jurisdiction, that would exclude Wardens from the Grand Lodge,
or allow appeals from the decisions of a Grand Master, or introduce sectarian tests,
or render a Master subject to his Lodge - but we think them general. They are
local when they commence, we admit, and so is a cancer; allow them to proceed un·
checked, and they sap the foundations of life. Nothing can be locally right that is
radically wrong ; more than this, nothing can be locally right which seeks in any
degree to introcluce an innovation or a change."
The opinion of our brother of Iowa that a Mason may not" demit" from the Lodge
of which he is a member, without a vote of the Lodge to that effect, we do not coin·
cicle with, as may have been evident from our previous reports; and we think that
npon reflection he will not consider the only reason he has given for that opinion as
very cogent. He says : "The brother enters the Lodge of his own free will, but with its permission ; he
has the same opportunity of leaving it of his own free will, but with its permission.
It required two to make the bargain for his admission-it requires as many, we think,
to make the bargain that he shall withdraw. The word' demit' itself means, accord·
ing to Webster, 'to permit to go,' and its very meaning settles the question."
Thus the general proposition appears to be that because it requires permission to
be admitted to a body, it must require it to be allowed to leave it! Because a ma·
jority of the votes of a district is necessary to admit a man to a seat in Congress,
must there be a similar expression of the public will to enable him to resign? Jn
our view a member has the right to withdraw from membership at any time, if his
clues are paid and there be no charges against him pending, by the simple annuncia·
tion of his determination to that effect; but that the Lodge may determine whether
it will or will not grant him that written or printed certificate of commendation usu·
ally denominated a" demit." As to the declaration that the meaning of the word, ac·
cording to Webster," settles the question," we can only say that to that word no such
definition as that above quoted is given by that lexicographer- he defining it "to let
fall, to depress, to submit." The word" dimit" receives the definition above present·
e<l, and is probably the one which should be used, though we can not understand why
the somewhat doubtful meaning of an arbitrary word, used commouly to express the
consummation of an act, should settle the question of the principle which ought to
govern that act.

ters, did not become the law.
"Had this carried," Bays he," and then the Indiana proposition become a luw, (as
it since has,) we should have considered that so far as those States were concerned,
Masonry was at an end. The three principal officers of the Lodges deprived of their
rights and their prerogatives, a revolution would have occurred which would have
made the Order something else - not Masonry."
Rather a lugubrious view of the subject, we suggest, as for some years past the
first regulation, which he thinks would have been productive of such lamentable re·
snits in Ohio, has existed in Georgia; and yet Masonry, an<l very good Masonry, too,
still survives in that State. And as to Indiana, we entertain little dou\Jt that the blun·
der there committed will, by its own consequences, serve to correct itself long before
"Masonry is at encl."

to the memory of the :Mjj,sons who there fell in their country's service; and a proposed
appropriation of $1,500 for that purpose - conditioned that a like sum be contributed
by Indiana-was submitted to the Lodges, that their representatives might be in·
structed in regard to its passage at the next Communication. The doctrine, now
general and, as we believe, correct, was ann<1unced, that a Lodge "may not be opened
for the transaction of any business unless the Master or one of the Wardens be
present."
A list of decisions by the Grand Master was presente.d in a condensed form by the
committee to whom his correspondence was referred, and they were concurred in by
the Grand Lodge. Many of these are so universally acknowledged th~t it is not
necessary to quote them here ; and many others are evidently upon matters regulated
by the Constitutional Rules of Kentucky, and uot involving aught concerning the
general laws of the Craft. To but a few, therefore, shall we call attention. It was
decided that "the Lodge under whose jurisdiction a non-affiliated Mason lives, iB the
only competent body to try him,"- that "an Entered Apprentice can be tried for
immorality, &c., the same as a Master Mason,"- that" any member of a Lodge may
prefer charges again.•t another,"- and that" a brother suspended for a definite period,
returns to his membership at the expiration of that period, without action of the
Lodge." All these we agree to, only suggesting that definite suspension ought to be
abolished. If a Mason is uufit to remain a member of a Lodge, the probal;ility of his
subsequent worthiness to return to it is not to be measured by a certain number of
months or years of exclusion, but the certainty of it should be estimated by his con·
duct after punishment. We think, therefore, that all suspensions should be for an
indepnite period, and th'at the Lodge imposing the penalty should have the power, at
any time, under such regulations as its particular superior may prescribe, to remit
the punishment and restore its subject, when atonement shall have been made or peni·
tence evinced for the wrong which caused its infliction. It was decided, also, that
"indefinite suspension and expulsion operate alike - both require a unanimous ballot
to restore,"-that "a Lodge U. D. may increase its members by affiliation, the same
as any other Lodge,"-and that" Officers of Lodges U. D. must be regularly installed,
the same as those of a chartered Lodge." These, if laid down as general laws, we do
not coincide with; but we do not doubt the right of each Grana Lodge to. enact such
regulations if it pleases, and we presume that tl1ese decisions are made in accordance
with existing regulations in Kentuoky. A further decision- that "a Mason living in
the vicinity of a Lodge, but a member of another far distant, iA subject to the authority
of his own Lodge, and not of that within whose jurisdiction he lives "-we admit to
be in accordance with the common opinion; but, for reasons which we presented in our
report for 1857, we believe it to be radically wrong, and effectual only to defeat that
justice in whose pathway no obstacle should be thrown.

its funds are derived from a monthly tax on each, proportioned to its membership,
and a certain sum levied upon each degree conferred. Its only connection with the
Grand Lodge has been that a copy of its annual report to its constituents has been
each year transmitted to that body as interesting information; and, as an evidence of
the appreciation of its charitable labors, those reports have been published with the
proceedings of the Grand Lodge.

At the Quarterly Communication in September, a committee to whom had been
referred the ·Address of the Grand Master in December, 1856, among other things,
reported adversely to his recommendation that the records of the Grand Lodge 'lie
printed. The report was adopted, but it appears to us that one, at least, of' the reasons given for the non-concurrence, is not in harmony with the usual wisdom and
intelligence which pervades the counsels of this ancient body. After declaring the
opinion that the advantages to the Fraternity of such a publication would not be
commensurate with the cost, the committee say" Our records are not intended for public inspection, nor would they interest the
general reader ; but in the hands of our enemws might be used t.o our hurt : during the
dark reign of anti-masonry they were sought with avidity, and with a perseverance
that would have done credit to a better cause, but which the Grand Lodge spared no
pains to keep from its polluting touch. Now what has been, may be reproducedthe persecution through which the institution has pai;sed, may be revived. Although
it is at the present moment, per se, a tower of strength, and apparently far removed
from danger, yet it not unfrequently happens, that we are exposed to the greatest
peril when we least expect it. Safety is the price of untiring vigilance and watchful·
ness.
·
" It is also greatly to be feared, that our treasury is not in a condition to respond
to so large a draft as would be required to complete a work of this magnitude ; and
if it were, the question naturally arises, is such an application of our funds in accord·
ance with the benevolent objects and uesigns of the Order? Our funds are sacredly
dedicated to the poor and indigent, and can not rightfully be applied to any purpose
which has not this object distinctly in view.''
Upon the first and last of the above arguments of the committee,- as being of interest not alone to the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, f.ut to the Masonic world, we should olfer some remarks, had not Grand Master HEARD, upon a subseqnent oc•

casion, presented our views in a much better manner than we ourselves could hope to
express them. In his Address at the Installation Communication in December following, he replies to the objections of the committee "It is said that the advantages would be disproportioned to the cost: what would
be the advantages? The diffusion among the Fraternity of the kIWwledge of the origin and early career of Freemasonry in America ; of much of its history here for a
century and a quarter ; and of the evidences of steady persistence in maintaining and
carrying out, in adversity and prosperity, our benevolent principles, by noble men
whose deeds and names ought not to be forgotten - are among some of the benefits
* * * * *
which will be secured by the publication suggested.
"It is objected that' the records are not intended for public inspection; would not
interest the general reader ; and, being in the hands of our enemies, might be used to
our hurt.' In the enunciation of these sentiments, the committee appear to have been
controlled by fears similar to those which actuated our English brethren to destroy
valuable records lest they might be seen by the uninitiated. In 1718 it was proposed
to compile for publication the history;charges, regulations, &c., of England, and the
Grand Master' desired any brethren to bring to the Grand Lodge any old writings and
records concerning Masons and Masonry, in order to show the usages of ancient
times;' and it is related that in 1719,' at some private Lodges, several very valuable
manuscripts (for they had nothing yet in print) concerning the Fraternity, their Lodges,
Regulations, Charges, Secrets, and Usages, (particularly one writ by Mr. NICHOLAS
STONE, the Warden of Inigo Jones,) were too hastily burnt by some scrupulous brothers,
that those papers might nut fall into strange hands.' It is lamentable that our transAtlantic brethren had so little confidence in the discernment and prudence of their
Grand Lodge ; for had it been otherwise, mu eh of the history of our Order would
have been preserved that is now irrevocably lost. Let us profit by this untoward example, and not neglect that which our successors could rightly claim of us as our duty. I propose not to invade the arcana of Freemasonry, nor to place ourselves in the
slightest degree in the power of our enemies, if we have any: on the contrary, I advocate the doing of that which will, while we preserve our mysteries intact, cement
together and strengthen the Praternity, and render us impregnable against the assaults of adversaries.

"The last objection of the committee is that which declares that our funds are sacredly dedicated to the poor and indigent. 'j'o this proposition I beg to dissent most
emphatically. Having already expressed my views as to the nature and objects of
our Institution, I will only obseJl've here that, though it is benevolent in its intentions,
and ·seeks to ensure morality among its members, its high object or distinguishing
characteristic is to cultivate the social virtues, and bring mankind together in the
bonds of brotherhood. Every thing that will tend to increase its social condition
should be made subservient to that end. If, therefore, the opening of .the pages of
our past, and presenting the virtues therein recorded, as examples to our brethren of
to-day and their successors, will contribute to that cementation which ' unites them
into one sacred band or ,society of friends and brothers,' any means that we can
command to effect an object so desirable, will not be misapplied."
The Grantl Master, in this Address, announces the issue of five dispensations during
the year to form new Lodges. Among these we remark "Hiram Lodge of Copiapo,"
at Copiapo, in Chile, the second in that republic under the jurisdiction of Massachusetts-the other being Bethesda Lodge, at Valparaiso, formerly under dispensation
from California as Pacific Lodge. He notices with approval the District system which
during fifty-four years has existed in that State ; and we remark the fact, most unusual
elsewhere among District Deputies, that every one of the eleven in Massachusetts
presented reports, which are printed with the proceedings. He makes the statement,
most creditable to his zeal and laborious industry for the good of the Craft, that during the year he had visited every Lodge in the State - then eighty-nine in number.
He expresses his disapprobation of that clause in the constitution of Massachusetts
which gives to District Deputy Grand Masters the "power to grant dispensations for
initiation;" and thinks that the Grand Master himself should rarely, if ever, make use
of this ancient prerogative. He relates a visit to the grave of the first Grand Master
of the Commonwealth, HENRY PRICE, (whose appointment, if we mistake not, was as
Provincial Grand Master for North America); recommends that a monument be
erected to his memory; and submits certain correspondence of courtesy with the
Earl of Zetland, Grand Maste'r of England.

Br-0. PIERSON recommends the preparation of a stone from Minnesota for the

Lodge; and expresses an opinion in favor of the formation of a General Grand Lodge,
in which he represents the views heretofore and again expressed by the body of which

popular with all the young Grand Lodges of the country- those which have not yet
reached their" teens "-except that of Nebraska, which as yet is.scarcely old enough
to speak, and of Washington, which was born but yesterday. California, Oregon, Minne·

while comparatively, in fact, entirely ignorant of most matters of then Masonic discussion,-in regard to which he was none the less still· required to write,-in his first
report in 1855 expressed an opinion in favor of the plan, for no better reason probably
than that the body of which he was a member had previously done the same. The
subject has since (and before too) been discussed tou widely to make it necessary for
him to state the reasons which in his case have induced a change of opinion, as _they
would be but a reiteration of' much that has many times been already written. Suffice
it, that while the attitude of most of the Grand Lodges of the country renders it certain that the organization of such a General Grand Body is impracticable, it is now, in

NEBRASKA.
The second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of this Territory was
commenced at the city of Nebraska on the second day of ,June, 1858 - the M.·. W:.
RoBERT C. JORDA~, Grand Master, presiding, and the R:. W:. GEORGE ARMSTRONG
being Grand Secretary.
The Grand Master, in his Address, announces the issue of three dispensations to
form new Lodges ; expresses the opinion that a Mason has the right to withdraw from
membership at will; and wisely suggests that now, during the infancy of the Grand
Lodge, a uniform system of work can, by proper care, be inaugurated and continued.
He proposes that steps should at once be taken to secure the preservation of the his·
tory of Masonry in Nebraska; and strongly urges the adoption of the Ohio test.
"I have observed within the pagt year," says he," a number of editorials and
reports concerning the belief in the Divine Authenticity of the Holy Bible, as II fundamental requisite to the Initiation of a candidate into the m1steries of Masonry. And,
strange as it may seem, in some cat<es a violent opposition 1s urged to such a require·
ment. * * * It is certainly a matter of wonder and regret that any intelligent
member of the Masonic Institution can, for a moment assume the position that some
have, and denounce this wholesome requirement of some of the Grand Lodges as a
'new test,' an 'innovation,' and other harsh epithets, when the ritual of the Order is so
entirely adverse to such teachings. And we are almost led to believe that those
taking sueh ground" have failed to duly appreciate the excellent rules and maxims
therein inculcated, and are inexcusably ignarant of the work handed down to us from
time immemorial."
Our opinions on the subject of this paragraph have been sufficiently often and at
length expressed in previous reports; and it would hardly be profitable to reprint
them. We quote this principally as an illustratiou of considerable coolness in argumentative assumption-the stating as an exception that which is, in fact, the general
rule. "In some cases" there has been opposition! Possibly there has, as of the
thirty-six (now thirty-seven) Grand J,odges within the United States, but three or four
have adopted the "wholesome requirement;" and one, at least, of these, with such a
proviso as makes the adoption meaningless. As to the "inexcusable ignorance" with
which AO many of us arc charged, we are content to suppose that in our own case the
accusation may be true; bnt we admit the profound sorrow which we feel in consequence, at being compelled to lose all faith in MACKEY, MORRIS, KING, BARBER, PEARL,
O'SULLIVAN, and many others, who have all so greatly" failed to duly appreciate" this
subject.
The Report on f'orcign Correspondence is presented by Bro. A. G. CLAltKE, and
him, also, do our regrets include; for the language he uses in treating of this question
in his report, indubitably places him among the "some," and in his other capacity as
Grand Orator we note his declaration that" Hebrew and Assyrian, Jew and Gentile,
Christian and Mahommedan, can kneel at the altar of' Freemasonry, and, in the perfect
equality of truth and virtue, vow allegiance to its trust.~." In still a third capacity, as
chairman of the committee to which was referred this portion of the Grand Master's
Address, he presented ce1·taln resolutions which were adopted, and which seem to
have been intended as a sort of compromise with the Grand Master, and to mean as
little of the Ohio test as was practicable with that view, inasmuch as they declare that
the Bible "from time immemorial has been one of the Ancient Landmarks, either in
the form of the Old or New Testament, or both;" and" that no man can become a
Mason unless he can avow a belief in the principles therein contained."
A resolution was a.dopted declaring that non-affiliated Masons, residing in a county
where a Lodge existed, wl10, for a period of twelve months, failed to apply for mem•
bership, should" forfeit all claims to Masonic rights or benefits." It was also resolved
that no voucher for admission should be taken, unless the brother vouching had been
previously in open Lodge with the proposed visitor~ a common rnle, perhaps, but, 'llS
we have before expressed the opinion, not always a safe or necessary one. The Mount
Vernon circular was received with approval, and the Lodges in the Territory were rec·

on the seventh day of December-the M:.W.·. PLEASANT A. HOLT, Grand Master,
presiding, and the R:. W.-. WILLIAM T. BAIN being Grand Secretary.
The Address of the Grand Master annonnces the issne of six dispensations to form
new Lodges; deprecates the injudicious policy of a too rapid multiplication of Lodges;
and condemns the haste with which many arc hurried into and through the ceremonies of the Order, as " a sort of Young American ism - a method of making Masons
according to the principles of ' manifest destiny,'- as if it was necessary that everything should be controlled by the same laws which govern locomotion through the
influences of steam, or the transmission of intelligence by the operations of the telegraph." He urges the adoption of some measure for the securing a uniformity of
work; and, having served in his present capacity two years, declines a reelection.
The Report on Foreign Correspondence is presented by Bro. WrLJ,IA:M K. BLAKE.
It reviews the transactions of twenty-eight Grand Lodges iu a manner which induces
us to feel regret that in most cases the notice is so brief. We observe that the claims
of Ohio and New York in respect to the origination of committees on Foreign Correspondence are altogether eclipsed by the statement that as early as 1789 such a
committee was appointed in the Grand Lodge of North Carolina. The views of the
Virginia committee on Jnrisprndence of 1856,-disapproving the reference of petitions
to committees of investigation, and favoring the introduction of honorary membership,- are not concurred in by Bro. BLAKE, and we need not say that we entirely
agree with him in the non-concurrence. A very flattering compliment is paid to the
labors of this committee in 1856, and we arc very thankful for it, as we greatly fear
that our present report will win no such commendation.
St. John's College occupies the usual space in the 11rocecdings. A fine and commodious building has been completed at a cost of $23,000, of which $13,000 is yet unpaid. A considerable further amount will be required to put the institution in operation; and, though we sincerely hope it may prove otherwise, we greatly fear that its
history will eventually be that of previous enterprises of a similar character-years
of expense, difficulties, and struggles, crowned with final failure. Seven hundred dollars were appropriated to it by the Grand Lodge, and a tax of one dollar for each
member was levied upon the subordinates for the purpose of paying off the debt. The
financial report shows that the receipts for the year were $1,717, and the disbursements
$1,994, of which $950 were for the college; leaving $49 in the treasury. One hundred
and twenty-seven Lodges are reported by the Grand Secretary, five of which, however, have neither assembled nor paid dues for periods varying from three to six
years. The Grand Lodge cloRed upon the fourth day, the 11f:. W:. AI,Fmm llfARTIN
having been elected Grand Master, and the R:.W." WILLIAM T. BAIN reelected Grand
Secretary.

"We are not disposed to continue his controversy with onr immediate predecessors,

the Holy Scripturee.' Individually, I am ut least half inclined to believe that brother

Without feeling any disposition ourselves to say aught further for the present upon

us, in the following words: "No religious test shall ever be rcqnired of any applicant for the benefits of Masonry, other than a steadfast belief in the existence and perfection of Deity; and no
Lodge under this jurisdiction shall receive any candidate without the acknowledgment
of such belief."
A committee to whom was referred certain matters relative to Relief Lodge, No. I,

The Committee on Gric,•ances report a case where a brother preferred charges
against another, which were not snstained by the Lodge, whereupon the brother presenting the charges appealed from the action had ; and expresses the opinion that
there is no authority for an appeal " in cases where the charges are not sustained."
Though it is not so recorded, we infer that the report was concurred in, and cannot
avoid suggesting that the position taken is bad law, and might often result in worse
justice. Appeals to the Grand Lodge, as we understand them, are taken from the
errors of the subordinates; and it may just as well happen that a Lodge has committed
a wrong in not" sustaining" charges, as in the opposite event. We are the more surprised at this declaration of opinion, as the numerous reports presented at this session
by the committee whence it emanates, are among the clearest and best prepared we
have ever seen upon such matters. The finance committee estimate the receipts of

Proceedings of the

[May 10,

who has been suspended or expelled by one of its subordinates, not only to his general
rights and privileges as a Mason, but to his memb~rshi_p in the parti?ular Lodge w~ence
he was ejected. He maintains the right, and, cons1dermg the q~est10n ~ro':'1 the ~om~ of
view in which he seems to have presented it, we not only cordially comc1de with him,
but cannot refrain from the expression of surprise that any opposite opinion should
ever have been entertained. Not being altogether certain, however, as to t~e ex~ent
to which he proposes that this doctrine should be carried, we take the occas10n bn~fly
to express the views which our ideas of justice commend t? our o';n unde~stan~mg.
In the first place, it seems to us that a perversion of terms, m speakmg of this sub;ect,
is constantly exhibited. lt is common to write of a Mason, whose sentence of expulsion or suspension has been reversed by the Grand Lodge, that he has been restored.
Such is not at all the fact. No trial is concluded in the courts of Masonry, any more
than in those of the commonwealth, until the tribunal of last resort, if appealed to, has
pronounced its judgment; and if that judgment sets aside the condemnation of the in·
ferior body, it simply declares the action of the subordinate to have been unlawful. or
unjust, and lea yes the subject of that action in the precise position which he occupied
when the proceedings were commenced. 'l'o say that one has been restored to that ~f
which he has not yet been deprived, seems to us an awkward use oflanguage; but, if
it be proper to call such cases" restorations," then every sentiment of justice, every
prompting of common sense should teach that the attempted remedy for error should
be complete. If the decision of a Lodge be illegal or unjust, and the Grand Lodge so
declare it, then from no part of the consequences of that decision should the party
implicated be a sufferer; for how monstrous would the proposition be that he who, by
the hi"hest tribunal, has been declared innocent of all oflence, should yet be adjudged
to suffer a portion of the penalty unrighteously decreed by the wrong-doing Lodge.
The reversal of a ju1licial decision plainly carries with it the abrogation of all its possible results· and we cannot inrngine what argument can be adduced in favor of depriving
a Mason 0 ;· membership in his Lodge, because that Lodge has been guilty of injustice.
Tims much for such cases of restoration, if reversals of erroneous judgments are thus to
be entitled. But there are instances where Masons may properly be said to be restored.
An expulsion or suspension may have been justly and lawfully decreed, and have gone
into complete effect, either for lack of an appeal, or by reason of the affirmation of the
Grand Lodge. Years afterwards, perchance, atonement for the error in consequence
of which he snffereLI, an amemled walk in life, an assured repentance of his former
unmasonic conduct, or any other cause which should make the expelled or suspended
brother a proper subject for Masonic clemency, might induce the Grand Lodge toterminate his punishment, and restore him to his rights and privileges as a Mason. In such
a case, we can see no reason why restoration to membership should necessarily form a
part of that act of grace. 'rhe original pnnishment is here acknowledged to have been·
deserved, and the culprit is conceued to have been properly placed without the pale
of Masonry and the Lodge. lt is therefore a sufficient act of mercy to replace him in
such a position as shall ern1ble him in the usnal manner to regain a membership; and
it would be an nndne exercise of power to force such a brother upon a Lodge, he having
no more claim to lie there than any other non-affiliated Mason. It appears to us that
these are the general principles which ought to govern the consideration of this sub·
ject; but, if our views arc erroneous, we shall be well pleased to hear the reasons why.
Bro. MAcn~Y urges the preparation of a Masonic history of South Carolina, and
states that he has long been engaged in the collection of materials for that purpose.
It is needless for us to say with what pleasure we would hail the reception of such a
work from his hands. He does not approve our usage relative to the qualification for
eligibility to the Mastership of a Lodge, insisting upon that part of one of the Old Charges which declares that" no brother can be a Master until he has acted as a Warden,"

those present, restore a suspended Mason, unless notice of the proposed action J1ad
previously been given, is strongly objected to by Bro. MACKEY-he declaring that. the
bv·laws of a Lodge give sufficient notice of its stated meeting•- that at such meetmgs
11 •Lodge may transact any business which is within its proper province - that it is the
duty of all members to be present thereat- and that those who fail in that duty have
no right to complain of the acts of others who have been more attentiYe. All this we
subscribe to as evidently good law, in the absence of any special regulation; but we
suppose that any Grand Lodge has the right to prescribe that notice shall be given in
such cases as that alluded to, if it deems it expedient •o to do; and this is precisely
what the Grand Lodge of Wisconsin has done. Its constitution reqnires that applica·
tions for restoration shall be made at a regular meeting, and that some subsequent
regular meeting shall then be named for action thereupon. This had probahly escaped
Bro. MACKEY's notice, as we do not suppose he would willingly find fault with the
Grand Master for deciding in accordance with tbe snpreme law of ltis jurisdiction.
The newly-broached proposition that all Masons flhould have the right to ballot upon
petitions for initiation in any Lodge, is not favored by our brother of South Carolina,
for the reason that it would contravene an ancient regulation; and sundry remarkB
upon the preservation of the work, conclude with the declaration that "an ignorant
and uneducated lecturer should no more be tolerated than a fighting parson."

CANADA.
The third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Canada was held at the
city of Toronto, commencing on the fourteenth day of July, 1858-the M:.W:. WILLIAM MERCER WILS01', Grand Master, presiding, and the R:.W:. THOMAS B. H.rnms
being Grand Secretary.
The Address of the Grand Master is one of the usual excellent papers from that
quarter, and we regret that a glance at it only can at this late hour be given. He announces the issue of sixteen dispensations to form new Lodges ; states that twentytwo Grand Lodges had acknowledged the legitimacy of the organization over which
he presides ; expresses his hearty gratification at the union in New York ; and devotes
considerable space to an illustration of the proper qualifications and duties of the
Master of a Lodge. He notices the receipt of a petition from certain brethren in
Demerara, for a dispensation to establish a Lodge in that colony; and gives the following very proper reason for having declined to grant the request:"It is very true that the British posse'8ions, both in Sonth America and the West
lndiP.s are, Masonicalf,. speaking. at rreSf'lll unoccupied ground, as no Grand Lodge
has y~t bee11 there established; hut did not feel that we, a :Sistn C'!lony:--ah.houg.h
Masonically independent of the Mother Country-:-.could consistently tnler!ere i_n this
mai.ter, even at their owu request.

The proud pos1t1on which we have attarn~d .rn the

Provi11ce and the means hy which it was arcomplisherl, are now matters of history;
and, alth~ngh we have successfully established our own Masonic independe11c"'., 1 do not
consider that we would be justified either in assisting or inciting another British colony
to follow our example."
Bro. WILSON recommends the early establishment of Provincial or District Grand
Lodges in the several Districts into which that great territorial jurisdiction is now
divided; and thus alludes to the negotiations which were again in progress for a union
with the " Antient Grand Lodge of Canada :""I am delighted to say that I believe your Committee, acting in strict accordance
with the IPtter and spirit of their iustructions, have been mPt iu a similar 11heral and
Masonic spirit by those Brethren with "horn they were appointed to treat, and that a full
and perfect understanding has !ieen arrived at; so that. in a few hours, I trust, a union
of the whole Canadian Craft-upon satisfactory and honorable tenns-w1ll be consummated, and all the Masons of Canada ranged under the banner of this Grand Lodge. I
feel that it is unneressary for me to say how 1, aided by many zealous and worthy.
Brethren of both parties. have labored to effect this great object; nor need I attempt to
express here the u11bou11ded pleasure whirh it will give me-before retiring from t.he
proud position which, by your kind favor, I have so Jong occupied-to hear that union
proclaimed within these walls."
The desire of Grand Master WILSON was fulfilled. It will be recollected that we
noticed in our last report the failure of the first attempt, in August, 1857, to effect a
junction of the two bodies. There was evidently a sincere wish on the part of each,
however, that a union should be accomplished, and renewed negotiations were
entered into. After sundry correspondence, the R:. W:.WJLLIAM C. 8TEPHE1'S, on the
part of the Gxand Lodge, and the R:.W:. THOMAS G. UmouT, on that of the Ancient
Grand Lodge, were empowered to arrange the terms of treaty; and, with the active

Bro. JAMES L. Eimr.rsH, from the Committee on Grievances, presented
the following report: To tht M:. W.·. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of C. D. UnL in the matter of
his suspension by Western Star Lodge, :No. 2, beg leave to report that they have had
the same under consideration.
The first objection taken by the appellant is that the summons served on him waR
insufficient, because lt did not appear on its face, nor by the proceedip.gs of the
Lodge, that the summons was given by the order of the W. M. It is not neceesary
that it should so appear, neither is it required by R11le 1, relative to trials - that rule
merely requiring the Secretary, in serving the summons, to act under the direction of
the Master.
The second objection taken is that it did not appear by the proceedings of
Lodge, nor by any evidence whatever, that any one, or a majority of the Lodge, were
especially notified and convened for the purposes of the trial. This objection is not
founded in fact, for the record shows that the meeting was specially convened for
the trial, and that it was held after due and lawful notice.
The third objection is that thirty-seven, being a majority of the members of the
Lodge, were absent and had not been notified. This objection also is not founded in

the

13

98

Proceedings of the

[May 11,

fact. There is nothing to show that even a single member was not notified. The
record shows that the meeting was held " after due and lawful notice ; " and in the
absence of evidence to the contrary, this must be held to mean due notice to every
member of the Louge.
The fourth objection is that the vote by which he was suspended is not a twothirds vote of the members of the Lodge. It is true that it is not a two-thirds vote of
all the members of the Lodge-but it is a two-thirds vote of the members present.
The appellant contends from the reading of the fourth rule relative to trials-" The
question guilty or not guilty shall be distinctly put to each member of the Lodge,"that a verdict of guilty can only be rendered upon a two-thirds vote of all the members of the Lodge. If this construction were to prevail, on account of the difficulty,
and in many cases the impossibility, of procuring a general attendance of the members of u Lodge, a guilty brother, no matter how deserving of punishment he might
be, would be very apt to escape conviction. Your committee conceive the true construction to be g·iven to the Rule regulating tri'als to be this :-that it is the duty of the
W. M. to see that every member of the Lodge who can possibly be notified of the
time of trial, is notified in due season; and this being done, that a two-thirds vote of
the members present is sufficient to convict.
The fifth objection is that hearsay evidence was received. The evidence alluded
to was of a conversation between a brother and the accused. This is not hearsay
eviuence, but is evillence of the declaration of the accused.
The sixth objection is that the affidavit of one J. VAN ScRAlCK was received in
evidence, which, the accused alleges, showed on its face had been dictated by
malice and revenge. The affidavit was clearly admissible, and its effect was to be
determined by the triers.
The seventh objection is that the verllict was the result of prejullice and ill feeling
on the part of tl1e members towards the accused; but of this there is no evidence
whatever.
The accused also appeals from the verdict itself as uusustained by the evidence ;
but the committee conceive the testimony to be amply su!licientto justify the finding
of guilty.
Your committee therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resolved, Thut the suspension of CHARLES B. UHL by Western Star Lode, No. 2,
be and the same is here by confirmeu.
All which is respectfully submitted.
JAB. L. ENGLISH,
E. W. ROBERTS,
L. BArns,
Committee.
WM. Er,wEr.L,
c. E. WJJ.COXON,

On the 18th day of March, 18iHi, the Grand Master issued his last order to the
Master of San Francisco Louge, i·equiring him to surrender the charter of that Lodge.
This action was based upon a petition addressed to him by all the officers, and twenty·
six other members of the Lodge, setting forth that for a long time previous, extending
over a period of nearly three years, there had existed antiigonistic feelings and ele·
roents in that body, which totally destroyed its harmony, and tentled to bring Ma·
sonry into contempt -that those signing the petition had hitherto cherished the hope

15

114

Proceedings of the

[May 13,

that time would heal the differences existing in the Lodge, and restore its harmonythat occurrences which transpired on the evening of the second day of February,
1859, had totally destroyed such hopes-that, on that evening, six petitions, one of
which was for affiliation, were before the Lodge for final action -that these petitions
were in due form, had been referred to appropriate committees, and had been favorably reported upon -that on the ballot being taken, all the petitions were rejected
- and that of these candidates, at least five were of spotless reputation, and every
way worthy of the honor they petitioned for. The memorialists represented it as
their belief that the applicants were not rejected in consequence of any Masonic objection to them, but only for the purpose of gratifying the unhappy feeling• hereinbefore referred to; and that the rejection was a great wrong to the candidates, and a
disgrace to Masonry. The petitioners therefore prayed for a dissolution of the Lodge.
This petition was accompanied by a statement of eight Masters of Lodges in San
Francisco-being all the Lodges in that city-setting forth that they were conversant
with the facts stated in the petition, and recommending that the prayer of the petitioners be granted. The petition was further accompanied by a communication from
the R:.w... Deputy Grand Master, who resides in San Francisco, in which that officer
said : " I am satisfied that harmony cannot be restored.''
On the twenty-fifth day of April following, twenty-one other members of the Lodge
signed a lengthy communication to this Grand Lodge, complaining that they had been
kept in ignorance of the intention of the majority to apply for a dissolution of the
Lodge, until after that step had been taken - defending the right of any Mason to
cast black balls against applicants - and denying any authority whatever to inquire
into the act or motive of such balloting. They further deniecl the existence of any
power to fix upon them, or either of them, the act of caHting the black balls in ques·
tion, or to exculpate the other party therefrom ; ancl prayecl that the charter might
be returned, and the Lodge be permitted to proceed with its business, as before.
The testimony taken before the committee substantiates fully the statements set
forth in the first petition, and also exhibits a lamentable, ancl, as we believe, an irreconcilable hostility between the members of the Loclge. We shall not refer to the
testimony in detail, but submit it for the information of the Grancl Lodge. Were the
occurrences of the evening of the second day of February last alone before the committee, and were we called upon to pronounce only upon the right of member; of a
Masonic Lodge to cast black balls, unquestioned and unconstrained, we shoulcl undoubtedly hesitate to recommend the revocation of the charter of San Francisco
Lodge. We believe, to the utmost extent that can be claimed for it, in the doctrine
that every member of a Masonic Lodge has a right to freely pass upon the claims and
character of all who may present themselves for admission at the door of his Loclge,
and to bar the entrance of any whom he cleems unworthy of that privilege ; and we
might even go so far as to recommend that no action adverse to a Lodge be taken
where even more than six men were rejected in one evening, against whom the majority of the members of a Loclge coulcl discover no objection. 'l'he power to cast
adverse ballots must be free and unquestioned, or the ballot-box will cease to express
the wishes of the members of a Lodge. Whatever evils may arise from the too free
use of black balls, they must be less than those which woulcl spring from an unmasonic inquisition into the motives that causecl them to be cast, or authorized attempts
to discover and censure those who cast them. Your committee place their recommendations upon a different grouncl -the entire want of harmony now existing, and
which has so long existed in San Francisco Lodge-a state of feeling defeating all co·
operation of its members, ancl destroying all probability of its usefulness. The great
principle of Masonry is harmony. Loclges are instituted to give effect to this principle ; and whenever any Lodge ceases to be governed by it, and exhibits only scenes
of strife and confusion, it shoulcl cease to exist. Such is the state of San Francisco

1859.J

I

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

J,odge. Only tlie power which called creation out of chaos could still the strife and
bring harmony from the discords that now distract that unhappy body.
Were it necessary, your committee might state facts which have appeared in testimony before them, showing the relative standing and Masonic character of the petitioners and the respondents. These facts are shown in the evidence and the books
of the Lodge.
. Jn the first section of the eighth article of the constitution of this Grand Lodge,
its power to revoke ancl annul the charters of subordinate J,odges "for such causes
as it may cleem sufficient," is expressly declared. Of the actual necessity for, and
legal propriety of, the revocation of the charter of San Francisco Lodge, No. 7, your
committee entertain no cloubt. They therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolutions : Resolved, That the action of the M:. w. .. Grancl Master in arresting the charter of
San Francisco J,oclge, No. 7, is fully approved; and that this Grancl Lodge does now
finally revoke and anuul saicl charter, and declare said Lodge extinct.
Resolved, That the Grand Secretary issue to each member of saicl Lodge, in goocl
standing, a certificate of dismissal, upon the payment of all clues charged against
him upon the books of said Loclge, at the time its charter was arrested.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Bro. JAMES L. ENGLISH, from the Committee on Grievances, presented
the following report:
To the M:.W.·. Grand Lodge of Califm-nw:Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of J01rn BROWN from the aetion
of Santa Besa Lodge, No. 57, in expelling him from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry, have had the same under consideration.
The first objection made to the proceeding, is" that the Lodge erred in not postponing the trial, as it was the right of the accused to be present thereat, and he was
only prevented by an accident which entirely precluded the possibility of his being
present." The accused has certainly a right to be heard in his defense, and in this
case he was heard through counsel of his own selection. It would have been an act
of courtesy, under the circumstances, for the Lodge to have postponed the trial; but
we do not think that the accused could demand it as a right. Notwithstanding this,
however, as we are always inclined to the side of' charity, if we could see that the
presence of the accused at the trial could, by any possibility, have had a tendency to
produce his acquittal, we would have recommended a reversal of the judgment, and
a new trial of the case. But, unfortunately for the accused, his presence would not
have availed him, the character and amount of the testimony being such as en·
tirely precluded the possibility of an acquittal.
The second objection made is that tl1e Worshipful Master erred in voting twice on
the question to proceed with the trial, the accused contending that his right to give
the casting vote only exists when he has not previously voted on the question, and
that under no circumstances can he cast two votes on the same question. Your com·
mittee believe the law to be that in all cases of a tie vote, (except by ballot) the Mas·
ter, in addition to his proper vote, has the right to give the casting vote. The limited
time allowed us to prepare our report, does not afford the opportunity to furnish
either authority or reason for our opinions. Upon this point, we will merely say that
such a rule has been adopted by this Grand Lodge in the new constitution, and we have
no doubt it is the declaration of the existing law as understood by the Grand LodRe·
The third objection taken is that the evidence was not sufficient to justify the ver·
diet of the Lodge. We have already said that the character and amount of the
evidence was such as precluded the possibility of an acquittal.
Your committee therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution:-

C. E. WILCOXON,

Which report was received and concurred in, and the resolution accom·
panying it was adopted.

To the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee, to whom the records, books, and papers of Valley Lodge, U. D.,
were referred, beg leave to report that they have carefully examined the same, and
find the minutes of the proceedings of said Lodge to be kept in a neat and proper
manner. Although the dispensation was issued to that Lodge in the month of July,
1858, but little work has been done, and the finances of the Lodge seem to be in
much too embarrassed a condition - the only business appearing at several of its
stated communications, being the appointment of a special committee to procure
loans in its behalf, and the reports of said committee that its effort.~ had proved unsuccessful.
Your committee are of the opinion that a charter should not be granted to any
Lodge until it affirmatively appears, in a clear and positive manner, that there is a
population within its jurisdiction sufficient to afford the requisite number of contributing members and unworked material, where by to enable it to have sufficient pecuniary resources to support the character and dignity of the J,odge. Entertaining
these views, your committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution : Resolved, That the dispensation of Valley Lodge be continued until the next Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Bro. HENRY F. "'WILLIAMS, from the Committee on Masonic Jurispruclcnce, presented the following reports: 'l'o the M:. W.·. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee, to whom were referred certain matters of difference between
Rough and Ready Lodge, No. 52, and Rose's Bar Lodge, No. 89, have had the same
under consideration, and report as follows: It is charged in this case that Rough and Ready Lodge had conferred the first de·
l(l'Ce of Masonry upon a candidate whose residence was within the jurisdiCtion of
Rose's Bar Lodge; and the evidence seems to substantiate the fact, but the circum·
•tances are peculiar. lt is shown that the party in question had once been rejected
in Rough and Ready Lodge, and after a probation of nearly two years, had again pe·
titioned said Lodge, and was elected. It also appears that the question of jurisdiction
lutd never been mooted, until after the applicant had been initiated. Under these
circumstances, your committee would recommend that Rose's Ba.· Lodge, No. 89, be
fraternally requested to relinquish its claim of jurisdiction in this particular case.

There are writers, however, who claim that Masonry was instituted by God at the

We have, on the other hand, writers who cliHpute the claims of the Craft to such

On the part of the Mason well versed in history and Masonic tradition, there is no
doubt as to our origin. The institution itself bears internal evidence upon the point;
and we can well conceive the necessity which existed at the time for the organization. King Solomon was about to enter upon the great and important undertaking of
erecting to God a house which should be " wonderful great." He had to employ in
its erection a vast body of workmen, upwards of one hundred and fifty thousand; and
a system had to be devised, by which order and regularity would be secured amongst
the workmen during the progress of the work. With that consun:imate wisdom which
has rendered him one of the most remarkable men the world has produced, he devised
the system which governs our Order. The design was doubtless derived from the
association of Dionysian architects which had existed in Asia Minor prior to the building of the temple, and which enjoyed the exclusive privilege of erecting temples,
theatres, and other public buildings. That fraternity was bound by secret ties, being
initiated into certain mysteries, and was distinguished by many peculiarities which
strikingly assimilate it to our Order. It is universally admitted that that association
existed in Tyre at the time of the building of the temple, and doubtless the cunning
man sent by Hiram to Solomon, as well as the other workmen furnished by him, were
members of that fraternity.
According to King Solomon's system, Entered Apprentice Lodges were instituted
for the government of the bearers of burdens, - Fellow Craft Lodges, for the government of the hewers in the mountains, the workmen in the quarries, the stone-squarers,
and the artificers upon the temple itself. After the completion and dedication of the
temple, all the craftsmen who were found worthy, were ailmitted to the Master Mason's degree. The system of government thus instituted by Solomon was perfect in its
operation. By it be was enabled to commence and complete that great work- the
most splendid edifice the world has ever seen-in the incredibly short space of seven
years and six months. And when completed, it resembled more the handiwork of the
Supreme Architect of the universe than of man.
The association was a vast fraternity of lmilders, in which each held that position
to which bis qualifications entitled him, and in which the brethren were advanced
from one degree to another, according to those qualifications. After the completion
of the temple, this same association of builders, or at least a portion thereof, was no
doubt employed by Solomon in the erection of' bis house, on which thirteen years
were consumed; as also in the erection of the house of the forest of Lebanon, and of
the house for Pbaroah's daughter, whom he had taken to wife. He also" built Tadmor in the wilderness, and all the store cities which he built in Hamath. Also he
built Betb-horon the upper, and Beth-boron the nether, fenced cities with walls,
gates, and bars; and Baalatb, and all the store cities that Solomon ha.d, and all I.he
chariot cities, and the cities of the horsemen, and all that Solomon desired to lnnld
in Jerusalem and in Lebanon, and throughout all the land of his dominion."
An association cOillflOSed of so vast a number, bound together as it was, could not
be evanescent. It had the elements of perpetuity in itself. And though, at this distant day, it is impossible to trace the exiRtence of the Order from y~ar tu year, or ~v.en
from century to century, yet from that day to the present, both history and traditwn
furnish us with facts which clearly indicate the continued existence of the fraternity.
:\\nat do we know of the early days of Rome ; of the kingdoms of Assyria, of
Babylon, of Greece, of Carthtige, of Nineveh, of J,ydia, of Media, of l'ersi~, or of
Egypt? Can we trace from year to year, or from century to centur~, the history of
those kingdoms or of their kings? A few of the most prominent pomts are all that
we know. And how many kingdoms were there of those days which passed away
without even leaving their names upon the record of time? If we know so little from
the pa 5e of history, of the kingdoms of those times, how is it to be. expected t?at
history should furnish 11s witl< an 1LCcount of a cotemporaneous associatwn of bmld-

ers? It could not be looked for ; and the absence of an authentic historical account
of the fraternity is no evidence against its antiquity. Though there is no question
whatever as to the existence of the Order for the last several centuries, yet the histories of the day are entirely silent upon the subject. When this is so with modern
history, so full and so ample in its details, what could be expected from the mere outlines which we have of ancient history?
Upon the completion of the temple, the workmen who had been engaged in its
eonstruction, necessarily dispersed to seek employment where their services might
be required. They were scattered not only over Asia Minor, but migrated to Greece,
Italy, and other European countries. Strabo, that old geographer, who flourished in
the first century before the Christian era, informs us that colonies were established
by the inhabitants of Palestine, on the Atlantic coast, about one hundred and uinety
years after the Trojan war, or about ten years after the dedication of the temple.
'l'he Phrenician fleets extended their voyages along the coast of France to the British
Islands; and, according to the Harleian MS., - a curious Masonic paper now on file
among the manuscripts in the British Museum at Loudon,-Masonry was introduced
into what is now France, by one who lrn.tl been at the building of Solomon's Temple.
Thus it was that the fraternity was tlispersed throughout the then known world, in
•earch of employment.
The first trace which we finu of tl1e existence of the fraternity, after the dedication
of the temple, is in the year B. C. 714, or two hundred and ninety years after faat dedication. In that year, Numa Pompilius, King of Rome, in order to carry out the design
he liad formed of beautifying the eternal city by the erection of magnificent temples,
amphitheatres and other public edifices, gathered together from Asia Minor, Greece,
and other countries, a body of workmen, and conferred upon them certain privileges
by the name of collegia fabrorum, or corporations of architects. The continued existence of these corporations of builders can be traced for upwards of a thousand years;
and their connection with the Masonic fraternity of the middle ages bas been satisfactorily shown by Clave!, a French writer. One hundred aud eighty years after
Numa patronized the fraternity, the building of the second temple was commenced.
This was in the second year of the reign of Cyrus, it being the five hundred and
thirty·fourth year before the Christian era, and the four hundred and seventieth
year afte,r the dedication of Solomon's Temple. We read in the third chapter of
the book of Ezra, concerning the building of the second temple, that "they gave
monev al8o to the masons and to the carpenters ; and meat and drink and oil nnto
them-of Sidon, and to them of Tyre, to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea
of Joppa, according to the grant that they had of Cyrus, King of Persia. "' • "' • "'
Aml when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the Lord, they set the
priests in their apparel with trumpets • "' "' to praise the Lord." The masons,
carpenters, am! builders here mentioned were of the Masonic Order ; for, according
to the tradition of Royal Arch Ma;;ons, the second temple was built by our Craft.
And here 11ermit me to remark that I have often been struck with the remarkable coincidence existing between our J\fa~onic traditions and the known facts of history.
That the Order existed at the time of the building of the second temple, we have
by tradition from another source. The temple, though commenced in the reign of
Cyrus, was finished in the reign of Darius Hystaspes, King of Persia. That prince,
during his reign, instituted au Order of Knighthood, which has been continued under

men in its ranks. The Order to whiclt I allude was known originally as Knights of
the East and West. They afterwards assumed the name of Knights of the Eagle.
'l'bey were found in Palestine in the days of the Crusades ; and are now known as

I have spoken of Masonic tradition as evidence of the origin and continued existence of the Order; and to my mind it is evidence of the highest character. Were these
traditions confined to our own country, or even to the country from which we derived
them, there might be some doubt as to their truth. As Masons, we possess a knowledge
of facts which occurred at the building of Solomon's Temple, unknown to the rest of
mankind. These facts, transmitted through a chosen few, are equ;tlly well known
amongst Masons throughout the entire world,- amongst men of all nations, creeds,
and races; and as these traditions in the different countries agree in all essential particulars, they cannot but be true.
The privileges granted to the brethren by Suma Pompilius, were long enjoyed
by them. Under his protection, and that of his successors, the Order flourished, until
collegia, or as we would now term them, lodges, were founrl in every city and in every
province. They were engaged in the labors of the Craft ; building cities, erecting
temples, amphitheatres, palaces and other edifices. As the Roman empire extended
its borders, the brethren followed; and throughout all the countries subjected to
Roman sway, splendid monuments of the enterprise of the conquerors and of the
workmanship of the Craft were reared, some of which remain even to this day, the
wonder of the world.
The Fraternity continued to prosper under t11e privileges conferred by Numa, for
a period of near twelve hundred years; until, in the fifth century of tile Christian era,
having fallen under the ban of the Emperor, Theodosius issuer] a decree abolishing
all 9 ecret societies, prohibiting their assemblages, and enacting the severest punishments for .all who should violate its provisions. 'rhis deeree was so rigidly enforced,
that the Order aud all other secret societies were, for a while, completely extinguished
throughout the empire of the East. l'l'ior to that time the Order had been introduced
into Britain. In the year 55, B. C., Cwsar landed and made his first campaign against
the .Britons ; but that people were not conquered until A. D. HO, when they were
subdued by Agricola, and the island, from the Friths of Clyde and }'orth to the
English Channel, submitted to the Roman yoke. About the year A.D.120, the Emperor Adrian built what has been known as Adrian's wall, in order to protect the frontier; and, as in the construction of all public works, the Roman Governors employed
exclusively the collegial J'cbrarum,or corporations of architects, I entertain no 1loubt
tllat the Order was introduced into Britain at that early day. We find no mention or
tradition of it, however, until towards the end of the third century, during the reign
of Carausius, who usurped the government of Britain. Albanns, a Roman knight- the
Saint Alban of English history, and steward of the household of Carausius,- patronized the Fraternity; and during that reign the Craft were employed ou many public
works. About A. D. 426,and ,inst after the issuance of tlle decree of Theodosius
against all secret orders, the Romans finally withdrew from Britain.
In the commencement of the seventh century, we find the Craft employed by
Augustine, or Saint Austin, in the erection of religious edifices. The old cathedral
of Canterbury was founded in the year 600 ; that of Rochester in 602 ; St. Paul's, in
London, in 604; St. Peter's, in Westminster, in 605; and many others were built by
hl~ about the same time. In consequence of the erection of these edifices, as well
as the building of palaces and castles throughout the kingdom, the number of the
Craft was greatly increased in England. About this time the Gothic style of building
was introduced from the continent. Masonry afterwards appears to have declined.
It began to revive under the patronage of Saint Swithin, who employed the Craft
in repairing the religious houses; and from his time the prosperity of' the Order grad·
ually increased, till about the year 872, when it found in Alfred the Great a zealous
patron. That prince appropriatell a seventh part of his revenue in employing a large
number of workmen, and re-building the cities, castles, palaces, aud churches destroyed by the Danes.

ulations were indispensably necessary to ensure its perpetuity. This mode of organ·
faation was adopted from that which had long been in force ill Scotland. In that king·
dom, James ll., about the middle ot the fifteenth century, granted to William St. Clair,
Earl of Orkney and Roslin, the office of Grand Master of Masons throughout the
kingdom, nnd made the office hereditary in his family. The Grand Master of that
kingdom beiug entitled, by a regulation of James I., to receive annually .£4 Scots
from every Master Mason, and also a fee at the initiation of every uew member, the
Earl of Orkney, in order to insure the collection of his f(•es, instituted the regulation
of requiring every Lodge in the kingdom to work under a charter issued by the Grand
Master; and this is the origin of' chartered Lodges. No such requirement existed
there previously, nor elsewhere, until the organization of the Grand Lodge of England.
The Grand Lodges that we read of prior to the organization of' the Grand Lodge of
England, were merely general assemblies of the members of the Craft, called by
the Grand Master to consult together as to its interests, for the purposes of
instruction, and to settle such difterences as had arisen, connected with the art of
building. The Grand Masters who called and presided over them, were appointed by
the sovereign of the country in which they were held. The power to appoint the
Grand Masters appears to have been reserved by the sovereign, when the Craft was
invested with its exclusive privileges; and, from the fact that that power was exercised until the close of the seventeenth century, l have concluded that the Craft were
not entirely deprived of their exclush·e privileges until that time. The Craft were
frequently allowed to select their own Grand Masters, subject to the approval of the
sovereign. It would •eem, too, that other general officers of the Fraternity were ap·
pointed by the sovereign power. Among the evidences to be met with, which go to
establish that such was the ca'4e, is the record of letters patent to be found amongst
the record of the Privy Seal, dated at Holyrood House the twenty.fifth of September,
1690, and granted by King James YI." to Patrick Copland, of lJdaught, for using and
exercising the office of wardaurie over the art and craft of masoarie, over all the
bonndis of Aberdeen, Bani'!', and Kincardine, to hold warden and justice courts within
the said boundis, and there to minister justice." This letter, while it tend>! to prove
what I have stated, that the Crnft were governed >'olely by their own laws and ens·
toms, also goes to prove that the officers who administered justice, according to :Masonic laws and customs, were appointed by the sovereign.
All the peculiarities of the Or1ler as it now exists are deducible from its ancient
character. One of those is that women are not allowed to be made Masons. Many
fanciful reasons have at different times been assigned for thfa exclusion ; but the true
one is to be found in the fact that women are not adapted by nature to the perform·
ance of those severe labors in the forests, in the quarries, an•l'on the edifices themselves, to which the members of the Craft were 8ubjected. And uot being constitu·
tionally able to perform the tasks, they were excluded from the privileges of 1he Craft.
At the preseut day, the study of the arts and sciences is only enjoined upon the
Fraternity ; but in olden times. the Masonic J,odges were academies of the arts and
sciences, wherein the brethren were instructed in all the learning of the age, and par·
ticnlarly in those branches connected with architecture, 'fhey continued to be such
schools until about the middle of the last century.

Fraternity, from its institution to the commencement of' the eighteenth century. 'fhe
limits of an address wonld not admit of detail, Since that time I"reemasonry has

say anything concerning the prineiples of the Craft. The interesting ceremony of the
