PART I.
Of the Organization of tlie Grand Lodge.
ARTICLE I.
OF ITS TITLE AND SEAL.

SECTJON 1. This Grand Lodge shall be entitled "'rhe Mo•t Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California."
S1w. 2. It shall have a Seal, bearing such devices and inscriptions as have heretofore been, or may hereafter be determined; which shall be affixed to all instruments
issued by or under its authority.
ARTICLE II.
OF ITS MEMBERS AND TmJIR QU AL!FIOATlONR,

SECTION 1. The Grand Lodge shall be composed of a Grand Master, (whose ad·
dress shall be l>Iost Worshipful,) a Deputy Grand Master, a Senior Grand Warden,
and a ,Junior Grand Warden, (whose addresses shall severally be Right Worshipful,)
a Grand Treasurer and a Grand Secretary, (whose addresses shall severally be Very
Worshipful,) a Grand Chaplain, (whose address shall be Very Reverend,) a Grand
Orator, a Grand Marshal, a Grand Standard Bearer, a Grand Sword Bearer, a Grand
Bible Bearer, a Senior Grand Deacon, a Junior Grand Deacon, two Grand Stewards,
a Grand Organist, a Grand Pursuivant, and a Grand Tyler, (whose addresses shall
Keverally be Worshipful,) and such other officers as it may hereafter designate; to·
gether with all the Past Grand Officers and Past Masters of tl1is jurisdiction, aml tbe
Masters and Wardens of the several chartered and duly constituted Lodges, or the
representatives thereof, duly elected as provided in Art. JI, Fart VII.

SEc. 2. Every officer and member of the Grand Lodge must be a member of some
Lodge within its jurisdiction; and with the cessation of such membership, shall cease
his office and membership in the Grand Lodge.
SEC. 3. No member of the Grand Lodge she.II be represented therein by proxy.
ARTICLE III.
0~'

ITS POWE:M AND AUTHORITY.

The Grand Lodge is the Supreme Mo.sonic Power and Authority In this
State, possessing all the attributes of sovereignty and government,-legisla1ive, execn·
tive, and judicial, - limited only by a strict adherence to the Ancient Landmarks of the
Order, and to the provisions of its own Constitution and Regulations.
SEc. 2. Its legislative powers extend to every case of legislation, not expressly
delegated by itself to the Lodges ; and the Constitutions and Regulations, which it
has an inalienable right to adopt and promulgate at its own convenience, and to alter,
amend, or repeal at its own pleasure, under the limitations therein imposed, are final
and binding upon all Lodges and Masons within its jurisdiction, until so altered,
amended, or repealed.
SEc. 3. Its executive powers include the granting of Dispensations and Charters to
establish Lodges within this State, and in other territory where no Grand Lodge exists;
the revocationc or suspension thereof; the issuing of special dispensations for all pur·
poses permitted by any of the provisions of this Constitution ; and the exercise, generally, of all such authority as may be necessary to carry its own legislation into
complete effect.
8Ec. 4. Its judicial powers are of two kinds :
1st. Original-Including the decision of all controversies between any of the
Lodges, or between one of them and a member or members of another, or between
members of different Lodges; and the enforcement of discipline upon its own mem·
bers, and upon the Lodges under its jurisdiction : and
2d . .App;:llate- Embracing the revision of all matters of controversy or discipline,
proper for Masonic investigation, which may have arisen in any of the Lodges, and
over which it has not retained original jurisdiction.
SECTION 1.

ARTICLE IV.
OF ITS COMMUNIOATIONS.

The Grand Lodge shall hold its Annual Communications for the trans·
action of its regular business, at the city of Sacramento, commencing on the second
Tuesday of May, at 10 o'clock, A. }I.
SEc. 2. Special Communications may be ordered by the Grand Master, whenever,
in his opinion, the welfare of the Fraternity shall require it.
SEC. 3. Special Communications shall be ordered by the Grand Master, upon an
application therefor in writing, setting forth the causes which demand it, and signed
by the Masters of at least five chartered Lodges.
SEC. 4. Every order for a Special Communication shall designate the object
thereof, so far as is proper to be written, and shall be issued to each Lodge and Grand
Officer at least thirty days before the day named for meeting; and no business shall
be transacted thereat other than that for which the Grand Lodge was especially con·
vened.
SEC. 5. The officers or representatives of at least fifteen chartered Lodges shall be
present in order to tr!msact any business in the Grand Lodge, either at an Annual or
Special Communication ; but, upon occasions of ceremony only, the Grand Master, or
his duly authorized representative, with a sufficient number of brethren to fill the
stations and places, may at any time open the Grand Lodge, and perform the cere·
monies for which it was convened.

AHTICLE V.

OF THE GRAND TREASURER.

SECTION 1. It shall be the duty of the Grand Treasurer1st. To receive all moneys belonging to the Grand Lodge, from the Grand Secretary; to give him duplicate receipts therefor; and to keep, in prop er books, a just
account thereof:
2d. To take charge of all other property of the Grand Lodge, except as provided
in Sec. 1, .Art. IV, of this Part, and keep an accurate account thereof:
3d. To pay ·all orders drawn upon such funds and moneys, under such regulations
as may be provided by the Grand Lodge :
4th. To attend the Grand Lodge at all its Communications, and the Grand Master
when required, with the books and all necessary papers appertaining to his office ;
and also, if required by the Grand Lodge or Grand Master, to attend with such books
and papers upon any committee which may be appointed to act in relation to the
fiscal concerns of' the Grand Lodge : and
5th. To report at each .Annual Communication a detailed account of his receipts
and disbursements, with proper vouchers for the latter ; and present a statement of
the existing condition of its property and finances.
SEc. 2. He shall execute and file in the office of the Grand Master, within fifteen
days after his installation, an official bond, in such penal sum and with such sureties
as shall be approved by the Grand Master, conditioned that he will faithfully discharge the duties of his office as prescribed in this Constitution, and, at the end of
his term, pay over and transfer to his successor all funds or property of the Grand
Lodge which shall have come into his keeping.
SEc. 3. He shall receive such compensation for his services as the Grand Lodge
may direct.
.ARTICLE IV.
OF TIIE GRAND SECRETARY.

2d. To receive, duly file, and safely keep all papers and documents addressed or

3d. To keep the Seal of the Grand Lodge, and affix the same, with his attestation,
to all instruments emanating from that body, and to all the written official acts of the
Grand Master :
4th. To collect all moneys due to the Grand Lodge, keep a correct account thereof
in proper books, and pay the same quarterly to the Grand Treasurer :
5th. To report, at each .Annual Communication, a detailed account of all moneys
received by him during the year, with a specific statement of the sources whence they
were derived ; and to present therewith the receipts of the Grand Treasurer therefor :
6th. To report, at each .Annual Communication, all Lodges which shall be in arrears
to the Grand Lodge, or which shall have neglected or refused to comply with any provision of its Constitution and Regulations :
7th. To conduct the correspondence of the Grand Lodge, and to submit copies
thereof, at each .Annual Communication, for its inspection:
8th. To attend the Grand Lodge at all its Communications, and the Grand Master,
when required, with the books and all necessary papers appertaining to his office :

SEC. 2. Each Lodge shall have not more than one stated meeting in each lunar
month, bnt may hold such other meetings as it may determine, or the Master shall
direct; but no business of any kind, except collections or appropriations for charity,

ARTICLE II.
Ot' DUTIES, PROIIIBITIONS, AND PENALTIES.
SECTION I. It. is the duty of every Master Mason to be a member of some Lodge,
and every one who, having resided six months within the jurisdiction of a Lodge, shall
refuse or neglect to make applica,tion so to be, or who shall not have regularly contrib·
uted to such Lodge an amount equivalent to its regular dues, while able so to do,
shall be deemed unworthy of Masonic consideration, and shall not be entitled to, nor
be the recipient of, any of the rights, privileges, or charities of the Order.
SEC. 2. No member of a Lodge shall be required to divulge his vote upon a ballot for affiliation, or for the degrees of Masonry; nor to assign reasons for such vote,
if it be known.
SEC. 3. No Mason shall hold any Masonic intercourse with an expelled or suspended Mason, with an illegal Lodge, or any person who has received degrees there·
in, or is a member thereof, nor with any Mason not acknowledged as such by this
Grand Lodge.
SEC. 4. For non·payment of his dues, a member may be suspended from all the
rights and privileges of Masonry, in the manner provided in Sec. 9, Art. III, Part III.
SEC. 5. For any violation of the Ancient Landmarks of the Order, of the Constitution or Regulations of the Grand Lodge, of the by-laws of his Lodge, or of any por·
tion of the Masonic or moral law, a member, or any other Mason within the jurisdic·
tion of a Lodge, may be reprimanded, suspended, or expelled, in the manner provided
in Art. IV, Part VI.

Grand Lodge, who may be within the State, and who is a member of a Lodge within
its jurisdiction.

Grand Master to transmit a copy thereof to the accused, if within the State, at least
thirty days, and if witbout the State, at le:ist ninety days, before the time designated

.ARTICLE III.
RELATIVE TO LODGES AND MEl\!lllCRS OF DIFFERENT LODGES.

SECTION I. When a controversy shall arise between Lodges, or between a Lodge

Lodges, charges maybe preferred by either party, if in good standing; which cliarges
shall be in writing, and shall be presented to the Grand Lodge or Grand Master, as
provided in Sec. 1, Art. II, of this Part.
SEC. 2. Upon the presentation of such charges, not less than five nor more than
seven Commissioners sliall be appointed and summoned, as provided in Sec. 2, Art. II,
of this Part, which Commissioners s!Jall be Masters or Wardens, nnd shall be selected
from at least three different Lodges not interested in the controversy, and most con·
venient to the parties ; and the accnsed pnrty shall be summoned, with such time to
answer as provided in the section an•l article last quoted.
SEC. 3. The Commissioners shall have power to proceed, and shall keep a record
of their proceedings and judgment in the same manner as provided in Art. II, of this
Part; and the penalties which they may inflict may be any known to Ma•onic usage,
or, if the case be one not involving a violation of Masonic duty, the decision may be
such special one as the circumstances shall, in their judgment, warrant.
SEC. 4. An appeal may be taken by either party to the Grand Lodge, as provided
in Sec. 8, Art. H, of this Part.

VACANCY.-Yacancies in office, either in a Lodge or in the Grand I,odge, may occur
by death, deprivation, resignation, removal from the jurisdiction, suspension, or expulsion.
JURISDICTION. -The jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge includes all Lodges and Ma·
Mons within the territorial limits of this State, and all Lodges and their members with·
out this State, acting under its authority :
The jurisdiction of a Loilge includes all ).fasons residing nearer to its place of
meeting than to that of any other Lodge within this State, except in towns or citie"
where more than one Lodge exists; in which case, each of such Lodges 11as separate
jurisdiction over its own members, and concurrent j1u-isdiction over all Masons not
members of one of such Lodges, who reside in such town or city, or nearer thereto
than to any other place where a Lodge exists.
REGULATION. - By a regulation of the Grand J,odge is meant any resolutiou,
edict, law or ordinance of any kiml whatever, other than the Constitution, which it
may adopt.
HusPENslON. -·The suspension of a Lodge h! an arrest of its charter, 11nd n tempo·
rary prohibition to assemble or work us a legal Lodge, until again authorized HO to do
hy competent authority ; and the act suHpends all its members except those espc·
cially exempted from its elli;ct.
The suspension of the Master of a Lodge is a temporary deprivation of his office,
and prohibits all recognition of him in that capacity, until he be restored by competent authority.
The suspension of a Mason is a temporary deprivation of all his rights and prlvi·
leges as such, and prohibit!! all Masons and Lodges from holding any Masonic intercourse whatever with him, until he shall be legally restored by the Lodge which sns·
pended him, or by the Grand Lodge.
EXPULSION. -The expulsion of a MaHon is the highest penalty known to the Masonic law. It is an absolute deprivation of ull tllc rights and privileges of the Order,
and prohibits all Masons and Lodges from holding any Masonic intercourse with him
forever, unless he be restored by the Grand Lodge.

for some speciHc purpose 11t the time aml piace therein indicated ; und it is the duty
of every Mason to comply with its direction, if he can, without great inconvenience,
do so.

GENERAL REGULATIONS.

L The practice of dueling being repugnant to the principles of Freemasonry, in
all cases where two brethren resort to this mode of settling their disputes, it shall be
the duty of the Lodge or Lodges of which they are members, or within whose jurisdiction they may reside, forthwith to expel them from all the rights and privileges of.
Masonry ; and no brother who may fall in a duel shall be buried with Masonic honors.
[Late Standing Resolution 31, May, 1854.]
2. All bodies purporting to be Masonic Lodges, held in the United States or any
of its Territories, within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of any State or Territory,
without authority from such Grand Lodge, and all the members thereof, are declared
illegal. [Late Standing Resolution 37, May, 1854.]
3. All Lodges within this State, having concurrent jurisdiction with other Lodges,
shall immediately notify such others of all applications for membmship or initiation.
[Late Standing Resolution 39, May, 1854.]
4. This Grand Lodge having recognized the principle-that no one should be initiated
into the mysteries of our Order, except in the Lodge nearest his place of residence,
(unless by its permission), and having, by an established regulation, taken care to
avoid infringing the jurisdictional rights of others, will not tolerate that its own be
invaded ; and it is therefore ordered, that no Lodge, subordinate to the Grand Lodge
of California, shall admit to membership any person who, being at the time a resident
of this State, has received, or claims to have received, the degrees of Masonry from
any source beyond its jurisdiction, without the proper permission, until he shall have
paid the Lodge to which he applies for membership, the full amount charged by that
Lodge for conferring the degrees, less the sum paid by him to the Lodge in which he
received them. [Late Standing Resolution 50, as amended May, 1857.)
5. This Grand Lodge recognizes no degree of Past Master conferred by any authority not holden under a legitimate Grand Lodge, acknowledging only the Order of
that name as it exists in the ceremonies attending the installation of the Master elect
of a chartered Lodge ; which Order shall be conferred on\y by a convocation of
Present or Past Masters, not less than three in number, who have thus regularly received it. [Late Standing Resolution 51, May, 1855.]
6. All Masonic communication between the Lodges and Masons of .this jurisdiction and those acknowledging allegiance to the Grand Lodge of Hamburg, is hereby
forbidden, while that body shall continue its unlawful and reprehensible invasion of
the jurisdictional rights of the Grand Lodge of New York. [Late Standing Resolu·
tion 52, May, 1855.]
7. Such standard of revenue shall be continued hereafter as will afford an excess
over the current expenditures of at least one thousand dollars; which excess shall
each year be set aside, as an accumulating fund, for the future erection of a Masonic

11 Jloard of Trustees, three in number, shall be elected, whose duty it shall be judiciously to invest all moneys set aside for such fund, and all moneys accruing from the inter·
t•Ht on such investments; and each member of said Board shall execute and 'file in
thu office of the Grand Secretary, a bond in the penal sum of $5 ,000, to be approved
by the Grand Master, Grand Treasurer, and Grand Secretary, conditioned that he will
f1ilthfully perform the duties of his trust. [Late Standing Resolution 69, May, 1856.]
8. All members of Lodges, the charters of which have been surrendered, who were
lu good standing at the date of such surrender, and whose dues shall have been paid,
11re entitled to, and may receive from the Grand Secretary, a certificate to that effect.
[I.ate Standing Resolution 77, May, 1858.]
!l. No Lodge under this jurisdiction, shall be allowed to transact business, other
ihnn the conferring of )legrees, with a less number than seven members present.
[May, 1859.]
10. 'l'he Grand Secretary is authorized to charge the sum of one dollar, for the
UHc of the Grand Lodge, for each copy of its printed proceedings for the current year,
other than the four copies to be sent to each subordinate Lodge, and those required
for transmission abroad, for future binding, and for the use of the Grand Lodge at its
1wxt succeeding Annual Communication. [May, 1859.)
11. All Masons, heretofore stricken from the rolls of Lodges within this jurisdicUon, for non-payment of dues, who have not been re-instated, are hereby declared to
be suspended, as provided in Section 9, Art. III, Part III, of the new Constitution.
[May, 1859.)

the State of California commenced its Eleventh Annual Communication at
the Masonic Hall, in the City of Sacramento, on Tuesday, the eighth day
of May, A. L. 5860, at 10 o'clock, A. M.

The Grand II-faster then delivered bis Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge of California, as follows:BRETHREN OF THE MOST WORSHIPFl:L
THE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA :
It is the fiat of Omnipotence that our passage through life should be made with a
velocity apparently increasing in geometrical ratio. The day, the week, the month,
the year, each seems but a tithe of its predecessor. Opened with the star of hope,
each marks its meridian with the hand of toil, and crowns its close with the fruition
of its morning dream or with a lesson upon the uncertainty of human anticipations.
We constitute no exception to this general rule. True, our faith in things immutable
leaves little chance of blighted hope, while our universal charity secures to us a more
desirable fruition than is the usual portion of the uninitiated world around us; yet
must we often drink the cup of sorrow, and tread the barren waste of disappointment.
Thus our previous life and thus the closing year have passed, till once again we
meet to compare our work, exchange fraternal greetings, and legislate for the benefit
of those who are to succeed us. We meet in annual convocation to correct the errors
of the past, to merge personal views in congregated wisdom, to bury prejudice,
and, by the electric current of fraternr.J love, to cancel space between the most distant, and fuse the whole body into a living mass, so that with one heart and one soul
we may enter upon the duties of another year, consecrated anew to the service of
Omnipotence in ameliorating the condition of man.
While such a past casts its shade before, and such a future beckons us to toil
anew, and vacant seats mark the place where wisdom sat a year ago, now gone for·
ever. to be succeeded by inexperience, we should be led to feel anew the incompetence of human strength and the blessing of proffered power Divine. And while we
meet the gathering hosts, the chosen of the Craft, each with a bow of hope upon his
brow, the light of faith beaming in his eye, and an open baud moving only at the
pulsations of a heart of charity, we are compelled to feel that there is a mystic union
here, and tliat all the power11 of evil combined cannot successfully make war upon
our Craft or set a dividing foot among us.
Thanks to Him who controls the destinies of man, that the past has proved this
true. Yo discordant element has been permitted to do more than poison itself and
die - no root of bitterness has flourished in our midst. The retrospect fa full of calls
for gratitude, and the future bespeaks a firm reliance upon Omnipotence - the one
our first duty, the other our only safety. The object of this yearly gathering stands
among human transactions alone. It has no counterpart in any other human convocation. In this annual meeting of the representatives of a great brotherhood, we
lose sight, for the moment, of the purposes which bring us together, in the heartwelcome feeling which words can inadequately express. If there be a fellowship of
minds, a sympathy of hearts in this wide world, which lifts us above the considerotions of self and nnites ns more closely than tlie common bonds Qf·friendship, tlwt

1860.J

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

283

fellowship and sympathy are to be found around our common altar. A sympathetic
chain, bright as the memories we love, binds us ever in fraternal union.
Our brethren of the ages past, generation after generation, have gone down to
the tomb, revering with their latest memory the lofty precepts which could fraternize
all races among men. The same principles live in our hearts, the same literature in
our teachings; and a Grand Annual Convocation of the time-honored brotherhood
increases the joy of meeting, by the reflection that we are perpetuating the same
lessons, and transplanting the same principles to the ages yet to come.
I am permitted again to congratulate yon upon the general peace, harmony, and
prosperity of our beloved Order throughout the world. At no period in our history
has the Grand Lodge convened under more favorable auspices. Our brethren every
where are zealously engaged in working together for the general good. The dissen'ions and party-isms, so rife in other affairs, find no abiding place in our Lodges: and
in all the fullness and appropriateness of the spirit and teachings of the frate~nity,
our members meet and act and part. Allow me especially to join you in thankful·
ness to the Supreme Ruler of the Universe for the general exemption of the members
of our Order in this Commonwealth, during the past year, from disease and death.
To this providence all good Masons bow in humble submission, not questioning the
wisdom of His ways, but ever grateful for the bounties He bestows. To His goodnes 8
we are indebted for the glorious achievements which our history chronicles in the
past, and for the enlarged advantages and substantial blessings of the present ; and
to Him alone we must look for health and strength and wisdom to accomplish whatever of good has been confided to human hands.
But few questions of Masonic law have been submitted to me during the past year,
tlie new Constitution having. provided for almost every contingency likely to arise in
the subordinate Lodges.
I must be permitted again to urge upon you the necessity of a thorough exemplitication of the work at this Commnnication. Many of the representatives of the sub·
ordinate Lodge~ desire to avail tl1emselves of this opportunity to acquire a correct
knowledge of the ritual as sanctioned by this Grand Lodge ; and, in the absence of a
Grand Lecturer, I know of no method by which a general dissemination of the work
among the subordinate Lodges can be accomplished but by a thorough exemplification in open Grand Lodge.
It is with much pleasure that I feel enabled to announce to you the termination
of the disagreeable relations which our subordinate at Honolulu, in the Hawaiian
Tulands, Hawaiian Lodge, :N'o. 21, has been compelled to hold, or rather not to hold,
with the Loilge Le Progris de l' Oceanie in that place, the Supreme Council of Prance
having at last evinced its recognition of that body as one of its subordinates. All
has been satisfactorily adjusted, and the most fraternal relations now exist between
those Lodges. Our brethren of Hawaiian Lodge seem to have acted strictly in aecordance with the instructions of this Grand Lodge, which authorized them to establish Masonic communication with the Lodge Le Progres de l' Oceanie, whenever they
should become satisfied of the lawful existence of that Lodge as a Masonie body. A
full transcript of the proceedings of the two Lodges has been transmitted to the
Grand Secretary's office, and it is herewi~h submitted for your consideration, with the
hope that the terms of the settlement may fully meet your approbation.
During the past year I have issued Dispensations for the establishment of eight
new Lodges, the names and locations of which will be furnished you by the Grand
Secretary. I recommend a careful examination of their work, and, if it meets your
approbation, that charters be granted them. The Charter of Yosemite Lodge, No.133,
having been destroyed by tire, I issued a special dispensation to the brethren of that
Lodge, authorizing them to work until the Annual Communication of the Grand
Loilge ; and I now recommend that a new charter be granted to that body.

During the past year, in accordance with the authority given in the Constitutio!1, I
have issuM several special dispensations to elect officers to fill vacancies in subordinate
Lodges, occasioned by a failure to elect at the time appointed by law, or by the in·
cumbent removing from the jm·isdiction of the Lodge; and to re ballot for rejected
candidates, within the year of probation prescribed by law. A full statement in ref·
erence thereto will be furnished you in the report of the Grand Secretary.
I have received and herewith submit to you, a copy of the proceedings of the
Masonic Convention, held at Chicago, in the State of lllinois, in the month of Septem·
ber last. The objects and aims of the Convention are clearly set forth in a series of
articles, in which it is provided that when they shall be ratified by live Grand Lodges,
notices shall be issned to the several Grand Lodges of North America, inviting them
to assemble in Congress at the city of Memphis, Tennessee, on the Friday next preceding the second Tuesday of September, 1862. Accompanying the report of the
proceedings of the Convention, is an address to the different Grand Lodges on the
continent of North America, earnestly and hopefully inviting them to approve of the
articles of association, and to meet them in the proposed Congress at that time. I
regret that I am forced to arrive at a different conclusion than that entertained by the
committee who so forcibly and cogently urge the necessity of a General Grand Body.
'fhe high Masonic character, however, of the brethren composing that Convention,
entitle their opinions and recommendations to yonr earnest and careful consideration,
and to such action as the importance of the subject and the interests of the fraternity
may seem to require at your hands.
I have received a communication from .Jom; CARi<OLL BlillNT, Esq., Secretary of
the Washington National Monument Society, requesting this Grand Lodge to render
pecuniary aid to the great and patriotic undertaking of erecting a monument to perpetuate and honor the memory of Washington. Tl1e work, which for a long time was
suspended, has been resumed by the society above named, under a charter from
Congress, granted in Pebruary, 185H. I feel confident that the patriotism and fraternal
·love of the members of this Grand J,odge will not permit this appeal to pass unnoticed ; and I earnestly hope that you will take such action in the premises as will aid
in the completion of a work so dear to every patriotic heart, and which has been hut
too long neglected.

California, has been pleased to appoint Brother ALEXANDER G. ABI>J,J, the Representative of the Grand Lodge of Minnesota near this Grand !Jody; and it has also pleased
the M.".W.". JOHN L. LEWIS, Jr., Grand Master of Masons in New York, to confer upon
him a similar appointment as the Representative of the Grand Lodge of that State.
It will be recollected that the R ... W.-.JAMER W. POWELL was appointed by my predecessor as the Representative of California near the Grand Lodge last named; and I

The officers of the Masonic Board of Helief of the City of San Francisco will
again present a flattering report of the charities dispensed aml sufferings relieved
through its agency during the past year, exhibiting a zeal and earnestness in its
1abors of benevolence which merit our warmest commendation. A similar Board,

fatherless and the destitute.

It 1111.s been the constant desire of your Grand Secretary to make the Library of
the Grand Lodge of California as complete, a.nil, at the same time, aH select a collec·
ti on of Masonic books as it was possible for diligence and money to obtain. 'l'he last,
through your liberality, has never been wanting, and such results as have depended on
the first, are now before you in two hundred and twenty·one elegantly bound volume><
of useful publications. A considerable number of French works on Masonic subject!<
were ordered nearly a year ago, but various causes have delayed their transmission,
anil the writer is thus denied the pleasure of laying them before you at this Communication. A large number of the annual publications of several of the Grand Lodges
of the United States are still on hand unbound, some for lack of a sufficient number
yet to form volumes of the usual size, and some for lack of missing numbers to complete the series, which it is yet hoped may be finally obtained. It has cost no little
correspondence to obtain so good a collection of those publications as that now pre·
sented, and the Grand J,odge may rest assured that, if life and health is spared to the
writer, it shall, sooner or later, be made as complete as possible. Since the republi·
cation, by the undersigned, of the earlier proceedings of this Grand Lodge several

of our American contemporaries have deemed it well to follow the example. The
Grand Lodges of Ohio and Iowa, and the Grand Secretary of Texas, have issued com·
plete reprints of the transactions of those jurisdictions, each in two handsome octavo
volumes, the receipt of copies of which have heretofore been acknowledged. The
Grand Secretary of Connecticut has already transmitted to us the first volume of the
"Records of Masonry" in that State, and is still engaged in the preparation of the
succeeding ones, which will include the entire transactions of its several Masonic
Gram! Bodies. In various other States similar labors are in progress, and there is
every probability that within a few years the complete history of most of the Grand
Lodges of the Union will be in our possession.
All which is respectfully submitted.
AI,J<JX. G-. ABELL, Grand Secretary.

In conclusion, we repeat the observation of our predecessors, that the relief granted to applicants " from California," includes only cases from without the city of San
J<'rancisco, as each Lodge therein provides from its own funds for the wants of its
needy members and their families; and again express our acknowledgments of indebtedness to both the Ocean Steam Ship Companies and to the California Steam
Navigation Company, for their continued liberality-the former, in making generous
discounts from their customary rates of fare to New York and New Orleans - the
last, in furnishing free passages in all their river boats.
All which is respectfully submitted.
LOUIS COHN, Chairman.

ALABAMA.
The Grand Lodge of this State commenced its thirty-ninth Annual Communication
at the city of Montgomery, on the fifth day of' December, 1859 :...the M:. W:. R.H.
rnRVIN, Grand Master, presiding, and the R:. W:. DANIEL SAYRE being Grand Secretary.
The Grand Master, in his Address, announces in fitting terms the decease of three
distinguished brethren; presents the plan for a" North American Masonic Congress" ;
Htates that he had refused all applications for dispensations to confer degrees in socalled "cases of emergency"; gives, as we think, an erroneous decision, or rather,
lack of decision, permitting the burial of a suicide with Masonic rites ; and expresses
the opinion (in which we fully concur) that " the Grand Lodge is not the most appropriate organization for the dispensation of Masonic charity ; but that this more properly belongs to the Masonic Fraternity in their subordinate Lodge capacity."
The Report on Correspondence was presented by Bro. s. A. M. Woon, Past Grand
ll!aster. It briefly reviews the transactions of most of the American Grand Lodges;
and we quote from it the following remarks upon the subject of suspension for nonpayment of dues, as they show the law of Alabama, in that respect, to be similar to
that of California, and as the opinion expressed corresponds entirely with our own:"Your committee regard the manner in which this question has been settled in
our jurisdiction as eminently calculated to subserve the interests of' Masonry. The
Master of each subordinate Lodge is empowered to have the brother in default more
than two years declared suspended. This jumps over charges, trials and all difficulties; but it does nothing of' which the brother has not had previous notice. And then
we find the further provision that payment will reinstate him. We are satisfied with
this, and cannot perceiYe where the inherent rights 1tre attacked. We are constrained
to say that we do not believe much in inherent rights. We believe more in declared
law. The last is at least most easily understood, and generally more uniformly followed."

Resolutions were adopted, referring the proposition for a l\Iasonic Congress to a
special committee, to report at the next Communication; directing the committee on
Jurisprudence to report at the next meeting upon the expediency of' so altering the
Constitution that the Grand Lodge shall have power, in case of the reversal of a sentence of expulsion or suspension, to restore the party aggrieved to membership; and
requesting the Grand Master to furnish annually a synopsis of all questions upon J\Ia·
sonic law which shall have been submitted to him, with his decisions thereupon,
Eleven Dispensations for the formation of new Lodges were issued during the year.
Bro. S. A. III. Woon," Historiographer of' Masonry in Alabama," submitted a report
showing that he was actively engaged in procuring materials for the fulfillment of tl:le,

ARKANSAS.
'Ihe Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of this State, for the year 1858,
was holden at the citv of Little Rock, commencing on the first day of November,the .w.·. W:. LUKE E. BARRER, Grand Master, presiding, and the R:. W.·. TROl!AS D.
MERRICK being Grand Secretary.
The Address of the Grand Master is, like every other paper we have seen from his
pen, an eloquent, well-written, and Jlractical production; and we again, as we have
more than once before done, congratulate the Grand Lodge of ·Arkansas upon its
good fortune in the possession of snch a chief. Although the warning contained in
the following paragraph of that paper is probably not so necessary in our own jurisdiction now, as it was two or three years ago, we still present it as a cant.ion which,
even at this time, is not altogether superfiuous
"I believe tliat our Lodges are multiplying too fast. There is too great a clesire,
whether from the bope of official appointment, or for the convenience of a few
brethren, or the gratification of sundry friends wh~ are. expecte.d to be candidates, or
from other causes, to locate a Lodge at our little villages, or neighborhood stores and
post-offices. We all know the danger of admitting improper materials to which new
Lodges are exposed, particularly when they are weak in nu!llbers, and have .no large
field from which to select. Want of money to pay for or bmld and fit up their ball-;
or rather, that which, by courtesy, is called their hall-and to buy jewels and f"m:m·
tnre, often leads to an increase of membership to the injury of the Fraternity; wlnlst
perhaps the old Lodge, weakened by the loss of members who have left it to form
the new one, is equally stimulated to increase its fold without scanning too nicely the
quality and fitness of the material. Let us pause then for a while, and complete the
old temples before new ones are begun."
A somewhat novel question, involving the proposition whether the political opinions of a candidate could constitute a legal disqualification, is thus most properly
re,;ponded to by Bro. BARBER:" I suppose that no political opinions can be pronounced a legal disqualification,
unless thev are such a;i lead to a violation of the charge concerning civil government,
which is given to the Entered Apprentice and repeated at the ~i:aster's installation.
Merely speculative opinions, however wil<l or repugna,nt to the gen~ral s~nse of ~he
community, can scarcely be so viewed. But there are other cons1derat10ns w):nch
mav well influence the vote of any member. For myself, I would consent to the ad·
mission of no person into our mystic brotherhood, however intelligent he might be,
however good his intentions, however irreproachable his moral character, if the
opinions entertained by him, whether p_olitical or otherwise, were such. as .would
proba\Jly prevent a cordial and fraternal mtercourse .. Some me~ of extensive literary
attainments, of good moral character, and of many virtues, are m some respects so
constituted by nature or education as to render them unfit for any social organization.
In such case, or whenever the general principles regulating the life and conduct of
the candidate were such as would not, in my opinion, promote the good order and
well-beinir of tlte Praternity, I should consider it my duty to reject him. 1 recognize
no one's rlght to become a member of our Order, and shall !(ive my consent to the
;i.dmission of none whom I can not receive as friends and brothers."

ABELL, (for 1858,) is the most elaborate and really instructive summary of the proceedintfs of the several Masonic Bodies of the 1.:nion we have met with, with the
exception of J<'lorida ; and, although, as we think, he indulges in rather unreasonable
facetwusness in relation to Arkansas, yet it fa done in a mirthful, kindly spirit, and
we forgive the sin on account of the sinner. The fact is tliat we foe! somewhat in
fault ourseh'es when we think of our own weak efforts in pre1iaring tbe present report
in comparmg the same with the diligent labor and discrimination shown by Bro.
AnELL in his report. The proceedings show tbat th.e Masonic sun in the ea;;t may
well fear that, without great labor and care, the star of Masonic lore and enterprise,
as of empire, westward will wend its way."
Our thanks are due to Bro. GALLAGHER for the fiattering notice, but it must have
been somebody else who indulged in the "unreasonable facetiousness in relation to
Arkansas" of which he speaks. Upon a retrospection of the report alluded to, we
do not find even a reasonably funny thing in that portion of it; and the nearest approach to aught which might Ile so considered, could be found only in the supposition
that we looked upon Bro. BORLAND's command of the poets as a joke-which we
didn't. The " new test" finds no favor in the eyes of our brother of Arkansas, he
considering it, as we do, a direct violation of the ancient and fundamental law.
Among the" Masonic Regulations" which are appended to the 1n·oceedings, we
observe one declaring that a ~Iason is subject to trial by the Lodge within whose
jurisdiction the offense charged against him has been committed, whether lie be non·
affiliated or a member of a Lodge elsewhere. This is not the general doctrine, but
we believe it to be the right one ; and we have more than once set forth onr reasons
for the belief. A report from Bro. El. H. ENGLISH, Secretary of the Board of Trustees
of St. J olm's College, shows that the edifice for tlrnt institution was nearly completed;
and concludes with the expression of a belief "that the Grand J,odge of Arkansas
will prove to some of the skeptical committees. on }foreign Correspondence of her
sister jurisdictions, that Meu<onry can accomplish samething for the education of the
rising generation, and. the elevation an cl improvement of the human race." As one
of the "skeptical committees" above aluded to, we avail ourselves of the occasion
to say that our unbelief did not take the direction ~uggested by Bro. 1"Nuusn. We
never doubted" that Masonry could accomplish "-Omething" could indeed accom·
plish very much in the cause of education; but we did, and do still, have very little
faith indeed in tlie proposition that the erection ancl endowment of a" Masonic College" is the wisest way to do good in that behalf. Passing by the opinion that the
interest of the capital invested in such an institution and the money reqnisite for its
current expenses, wonld be productive of more real good if employed in giving the
rudiments of education to many, rather than in perfecting a collegiate course for n
few ,-we are inclined to believe that the same revenue would educate annually more
and better scholars at some one of the numerous well-endowed seminaries of learning already in existence. The experience of Kentucky and Missouri !ms probably
demonstrated that; and we can only say that we lnost sincerely hope that that of
our brethren of Arkansas will be of a very different character.

T·he Grand Master, in his Address, presents certain correspondence with the Earl
of Zetland, relative to a question of jurisdiction; notices the union in Canada and
New York; refers to the M"ount Vernon subject; and announces the issue of five Dis·
pensations to form new Lodges. The following remarks in relation to the rights
acquired by an applicant, after having received the first degree, are entirely in con·
sonance with the opinions w.hich we have constantly advocated, which we have· in
part succeeded in engmfting upon our own organic law, and which, in the fullness of
time, we hope to sec admitted tliere in full:"A practice prevails to a considerable extent tliroughout the Lodges in this jurisdiction, of requiring a ~lear ballot before a. brother can be advanced to a superior
degree. This practice has created some discord in sevcr·al of our Lodge", and has
given rise to questions of the propriety ot' this course. These questions have been
repeat~dly submitted to me for decision. The opinion which I have given is, that no
I,odge is doing right that denies advancement to a brother upon the result of the
secret ballot alone. The question of the admission of it candidate upon liis first application is one which every member has a right to pass upon by the secret ballot.
This right is sacred and unquestioned. The candidate has voluntarily submitted himself for acceptance or rejection, he has no rights to claim at the liands ol' tlie Lodge,
his cliaracter must stand the test with everv individual member whatever be the
result. But upon the question of advancement, a far dif!erent state of things exists.
By initiation, the candidate becomes a Mason and a brother; he is made amenaole to
our laws and regulations, and in the Lodge has certain rights and privilei{es ; and
'one of those rights is, that before conviction of any offense, he may claim a trial
before his peers.' No man makes application to a Lodge for the first degree of
Masonry alone, nor the first and second, hut for all the degrees of' symbolic Masonry.'
His petition is 'to become a member of our ancient institution,' ancl having been
notified of his acceptance by the Lodge, and received the first impreRs of our institution, lie is entitled to a fulfilment of the implied contract, unless 11pon due examination he is found by his own acts to be unworthy. The position which I here take is
sustained by Masonic breth1·en of distinguished ability, whose familiarity with the true
principles of our Order and unremitting researches in Masonic literature entitle their
opinions to great weight. I quote l'rom the address of JM':. iv:. ALEX'R H. P!:TNEY,
made to this Grand Lodge at its annual communication in May, 1848. He says-' I
do most unequivocally repudiate the doctrine that a Lodge is doing right to deny
advancement to an Entered Apprentice provided he shall not be impeached for any
offense committee! subsequent to hiA acceptance.' Also from the Freemason's Monthly Magazine, by R:.iv... CHARJ.>os W. Mo01uo, (Vol. 9, page 327,) 'A candidate may
be rightfully debarred the privilege of advancing to a superior degree for any cause
that if known would have prevented his admiRsion to the first degree-a oubstantive
reason must be given; and it must be such as wonla sustain a char~e against his
moral character; of its sufficiency however the Lodge fa to determine. Like views
are entertained by the Masonic Review, (Vol. 4, page 26.) This position is also sus·
tained by Sec. 51 of the by· laws of the Grand Lodge of the State of Jllinois-to wit:
' one ballot on a petition to be ma•le a Mason, if clear, entitleH the applicant to the
three degrees of Symbolic llfasonry.' ''

"Tlie Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia, in 1823, adopted resolutions favoring

" On the day designated by the above resolution, delegates were in attendance
from the Grand J"odges of .Alabama, Connecticut, District of Columbia, ~fassachu­

"One of the first questions that came before the Convention was npon the admission of the delegates from Michigan. It was referred to a committee who reported
adversely to the recognition of the Grand Lodge of Michigan, which report was
unanimously concurred in by the Convention. That action of the Convention, although acknowledged by the Grand Lodges (Ohio excepted) to be correct, was used
by those opposed to a General Grand J,odge as an argument against the organization
of such a body. The convention considered six subjects, coming within the scope of
the resolution under which they were appointed: 1. Uniformity of work; 2. The
Represent>ttive system; 3. Necessity of Grand Lodge certificates; 4. Ueceiving
promissory notes for degrees conferred; 5. Transaction of Masonic Business in
Lodges below the degree of Master Mason; 6. U1ion the grade of penalty to he inflicted for the non-payment of dues by members of subordinate Lodges.
"These were questions, particularly the last three, of great importance to the
Craft every where. The act10n taken proved the a(lvantage that could be derived
from a Grand Body having authority to speak upon those and kindred matters. Upon
Uniformity of Work, the convention recommended a convention of skillful brethren,
one or more from each Grand Lodge, to be styled Grand Lec,turers, to meet together
onee in three years to compare their lectures and to correct variations. In accordance with the recommendation, delegates from sixteen Grand Lodges met at Baltimore in May, 1843. Bro. JouN DovE, of Virginia, was elected Chairman. It has been
"npposed that they agreed upon a Hystem of work; but if they rli<l, it has not been
llromulgated to the Craft. Each delegate reported upon his return !1ome that the
work he had formerly taught had been adopted with slight variations, except some
new things. 'l'wo Text Books, differing materially, were issued, each claiming to he
the work adopted. I have heard a dozen variations of the Lectures, each declared to
be such as were agreed upon at llaltimore. W11at with the introduction of new
'Signs,' 'Due Guards,' aud 'hifihest pinnacles,' &c., &c., more discrepancies existed in
the work two years after the Convention than did two years previously. A new system is a paying institution-but I am digressing.
"'l'he Convention proposed a.Grand l\fasonic Convention to meet triennially, and a
set of (eight) R.ules for the government thereof, to go into effect when thirteen Grand
Lodges approved of them ; and adjourned to meet at Winchester, Virginia, in 1846.
The meeting did not take place ; the Grand Lodges i:;ppear to have been •atisfied

(in 1845), the Grand Lodge of Maryland proposed a convention to meet in Baltimore

for evident justice, has gone into almost universal usage ; and had we not already
expressed our opinions at some length upon this subject in our last report, not even
our feeble health should prevent us from now lifting up onr voice against a proposition so utterly violative of every sentiment of right. The Jinancial accounts exhibit

NORTH CAROLINA.
Our latest intelligence from the Grand Lodge of North Carolina is of its Annual
Communication for the year 1858, commenced at the city of Raleigh on the sixth day
of December-the M.·. W.·. ALFRED MARTIN, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·.
W.·. WILLIAM T. BJ.IN being Grand Secretary.

1860.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

325

The Grand Master, in his Address, announces the issue of six Dispensations to form
new Lodges; urges renewed efforts on behalf of the Masonic College, which, to use
his own language," like all the great works that have been undertaken in our dear
old State has languished from its very inception"; regrets the numerous expulsions
and suspensions which occurred during the year, as being evidence of a lack of "that
rigid scrutiny" into the character of applicants for admission, which "a prudent regard for the harmony aml true prosperity of the J,odges, and for the interest and
honor of the Order, requires"; and recommends no recognition of the Grand Lodge
of Canada until the lawful existence of that body shall be acknowledged by the
Grand Lodge of England-a recommendation which was approved. After pointing
out the great mischief done the institution by the careless or criminal admission of
unworthy men, he well presents the probably greater evil resulting to it from the
ignorance and incapacity of those sometimes occupying the highest stations in the
Lodges, as follows: "There is another class, differing very essentially from that of' which we have
been treating, who, though influenced by better motives, have brought upon the In·
stitution consequences even more pernicious, the primary cause of' which is a deficiency in the qualification of our officers. This class prob3.bly had some slight con·
ception of what Masonry really is, and an honest purpose in embracing it, but have
been disappointed through the incapacity ol' the officers to present it in its true char·
acter, or to give even a distinct outline of what it really is. They have, therefore,
abandoned it, or so "damn it with faint praise,'' that open and avowed hostility
would be a more merciful infliction: for such arc often meu who have a character, in
the community, for honesty of purpose, and for a correct appreciation of what is
good and virtuous; and when such are indifferent, lukewarm, or hostile, the evil consequences are incalculable. For the mischief consequent upon the influence of the
fir.it of these two classes, there is only a palliative, which, as I have suggested, consists in a more rigid scrutiny into the character of all applicants; and for tl1e latter,
I hope and believe a cnre. This can only be effected by a thorough knowledge of
the Work, the Lectnres, and the true and comprehensive principles of Masonry, which
every Master should be capable of communicating. Of the manifold disadvantages,
against which the Institution has continually to struggle, those arising from incapacity
of its officers are notoriously preeminent. This condition of things '!tangs like a pall
over the spirit of Masonry. For this, l1owevcr, the officers are not always censurable.
The lack of opportunities to learn, or the natural ability to retain, and to impart instruction, can be plead in their behalf. But wit11 too many, the acquisition of office
is the chief object of their ambition; this attained they are therewith content. To
the officers, then, and through them to the Grand Lodge, we must appeal for the
means of relieving the Institution from the constantly accumulating evils, resulting
from defective teaching, or the lack of ability to t<iaclt at all. The ability to confer
the degrees, and to give the lectures antl charges co1-rectly and impressively, is the
first great essential; for these are the first lessons placed before the candidate, and
witllout a knowledge of which he cannot in reality advance. But when this is done,
and even well done, what have we then placed before him? Simply a very beautiful
piece of statuary- a perfect Apollo in symmetry and grace; beautiful and interesting
to contemplate for a season. But to inspire our love~ our ardent, sincere, and constant devotion, it must be animated by a soul worthy of such a body. This requires
but a thorongh understanding and constant practical exemplification of tl1e pnre and
:mblime principles of Masonry. It wants but these to warm it into life-to infuse
into it that all-pervading influence that touches the heart, and before which the evil
passions and guilty purposes dissolve and pass away like the noxious vapors of night
before the morning sun. How important, then, that he who assumes the office of
master and teacher of such a work, should po~sess the ability, not only to do the
work correctly, but to give it vitality- to explain its origin, organization and purposes, the laws by which it is governed, and by which it governs, but that his own life
and conduct should be a perfect exemplification of true Masonic principles. The
rapid spread of Masonry, with the neglect of these important considerations, is fast
reducing it to the standard of ordinary societies, and the uninitiated are losing their
reverence for the name of Mason, while thousands who have been hurried through its
courts, with but a glimpse of it~ most prominent points, first cease to admire, having
never learned to understand, and consequently to Jove; then lose all interest in it,
and finally demit, and are no more seen in its private councils or public assemblies."

beneficence that can supply its place? Who will care for the orphans thus again

of secondary importance; and further hope that his advancement to tlie highest office
in the Grand Lodge, has not been the incentive to that •zeal for Masonry' displayed
t1y him in former yearn, but that he was actuated by higher and nobler motives."

PENNSYLVANIA.

The publication before us presents an" abstract of the proceedings" of the Grand
Lodge of this State during the year 1858, including two Quarterly Communications,
a special Communication on the occasion of the death of the R:.W:. JOHN K. MITCHELL, Grand Master, and the Annual Communication on the day of St. John the Evangelist; all held in the city of Philadelphia, and at the two last of which the R:. W:.
HENRY M. PHILLIPS, Deputy Grand Master, and afterwards Grand Master, presided,
the R:.W.-. WILLIAM H. ADAMS being Grand Secretary.
An Installation Address was delivered by the Grand Master at the meeting last
named, in which the decease of his predecessor was properly noticed, the issue of
warrants for the formation of sixteen new Lodges was announced, and other matters
of local importance only were presented.
A Report on Correspondence, of considerable length, was presented by Bro.
RICHARD VAUX- devoted principally to an exhibition of the various communications
between the Correspondence Committees of Pennsylvania and New York relative
to the late non-intercourse between the Grand Lodges of those States, now happily
at an end. Some pages, however, are given to a defence of his Grand Lodge against
the charges of isolation, insularity, and exclusiveness which, not altogether
unjustly, as we are inclined to think, have heretofore been presented from other
jurisdictions. The advocacy has certainly been committed to a skillful hand, and the
work exhibits a pleasing combination of literary ability and Masonic forbearance.
Yet the defence scarcely disproves the indictment, and is rather a justification than a
denial. He deprecates so much Masonic publication; believes not in "Masonic Congresses, or any other like novelties, which might impair the attachment of the Craft
to their immediate jurisdictions"; and does not approve of the proceedings which
brought about the late union in Canada and the establishment of the present Grand
Lodge of that Province.
A subscription to the Mount Vernon Fund was declined on account of the heavy
existing liabilities of the Grand Lodge, the outstanding loans still amounting to about
$125,000. The total revenue for the year, from dues, rents, &c., was $35,955, and the
entire expenditure $32,150, of which some $23,000 was for principal and interest paid
on the debt above alluded to. The "Stephen Girard Charity Fund" is reported as
now amounting to $39,000, from the income of which $2 ,000 was appropriated for the
particular charities to which this fund was dedicated. There is besides a " Grand
Lodge Charity Fund" of large amount, from which it appears that $1,370 had been
disbursed by its Almoners during the year. A list of Lodges, but none of membership, is given in this publication. From this we learn that one hundred and sixty-one
subordinates acknowledge the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania. As
before stated, the R:.W:. HENRY M. PHILLIPS was elected Grand Master, and the
R:. W:. WILLIAM H. ADAMS was reelected Grand Secretary.

VERMONT.
The Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of this State for the year 1859,
was commenced at the town of Burlington on the twelfth day of January- the M.·.
w. .. PHILIP c. TUCKER, Grand Master, presiding, und the R ... w... JOHN B. HOLLENBECK being Grand Secretary.
The Address of the Grand Master is, as usual, an interesting paper; though perhaps the discussion of some little details, like the prices of sashes and collars, might
perchance have found more appropriate place in the report of some committee. He
announces the issue of dispensations to form two new Lodges ; and the suspension
of an old one by his order, in consequence of its disobedience of a mandate of the
Grand Lodge -an act so entirely approved by that body that the charter of the contumacious Lodge was subsequently revoked. He suggests an alteration of the clothing of the Grand Officers, which is now "purple trimmed with gold," stating that he
knows "of no good reason for the adoption of this color, as it is certainly not the
appropriate color of the Master's degree, and why it was adopted originally" he is
not informed. What may be the particular color (if indeed there be such a one)
which should be worn by a Grand Lodge, we do not pretend to give any opinion concerning; but we are inclined to think that the reason why this one has been generally
adopted is not very difficult to find. From the earliest periods purple has been considered the peculiar color of authority or of sovereignty. We read of the "purple
raiment" worn by ancient Kings, or bestowed by them as a mark of especial distinction; and the assumption of the "imperial purple" was but a synonyme for accession to the throne of the Roman Emperors. The. selection of this color, therefore,
for the body holding sovereign power in Masonry, is so far from being unaccountable,
that it would rather seem singular that any other should be adopted. Yet there is
certainly no other reason why the Grand Lodge of Vermont shoulU not wear "gold
bullion lace" instead of purple velvet, if its taste inclines in that direction. The
clothing of the Grand Lodge of England is white, and the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, if we recollect aright, has lately followed its example. If there is any "appropriate color for the Master's degree," which has any particular claim for consideration in such a case, founded upon the traditions and lessons of the order, it is
probably this one, and not that to which Bro. TUCKER undoubtedly alludes. It is true
that, in modern times, in England and the United States, usage has made blue the
color of the Lodges. But we have not yet learned that there is any other authority
for this; and it is very certain that in Scotland, some of whose Lodges were permanent long before a stationary Lodge existed in the southern Kingdom, the subordinates severally adopt such colors as they please, while the Grand Lodge is clothed
in green. We are much gratified at learning that Grand Master TucKER and the
Grand Secretary, Bro. HOLLENBECK, are engaged upon a '' history of the Grand Lodge
of Vermont since 1794, and of the Masonry which preceded the formation of that
body in that State," and that they hope within a year or two to announce its completion. Such a work would be interesting for its facts alone, but it will be rendered
doubly so as coming from such a source. The Address contains an account of the
lectures of Freemasonry, as introduced into the United States, which we deem sufficiently instructive to authorize the following extract: "About the year 1800-twelve years after the publication of PRESTON'S' Illustrations '-an English brother, whose name I have been unable to obtain, eame to Boston, and taught the English Lectures as they had been arranged by PRESTON. saic law, when divested of idolatry; and the Christian revelation. Again, in 1772,
these lectures were revised and improved by PRESTON, whose system was the stand·
ard in England until the Union of 1813, wheu Dr. HEMMING established the system now
generally practised in the English Lodges.'

A long and ver.y interesting Report on Correspondence was presented by Bro. L. C.
BUTLER; but, though we have read it with great pleasure, causes already indicated
will prevent us from giving it more than' a passing notice. A lengthy extract from
the Address of our Grand Master, Bro. CURTIS, in 1858, is llattel'ingly quoted; and a
compliment is bestowed upon our report of that year. The writer has fallen i_nto two
errors, however, in saying that we argued "against the long established rule of Ma·
sonry that no appeal can be taken from a Master's dccision,-regarding it as an ex·
ercise of despotic power to allow a Master' to maintain his single opinion in opposition, as it may be, to the united voice of the body which created him.' " In the first
place, there is no" long established rule of Masonry tl1at no appeal can be taken
from a Master's decision." On the contrary, such a decision may always be appealed
from to the Grand Lodge or Grand Master. In the second place, the remarks which
he quotes had no reference whatever to a J,odge or a" Master," but distinctly refer·
red to the Grand Lodge and Grand Master. We never dreamed of questioning the
propriety of the usage that there should be ·no appeal from the Master to bis Lodge,
for the reason that there is a higher authority to which an appeal may be taken; but
we did, and do still, suggest that it is nothing less than an absurdity that in a Grand
Lodge, a body beyond which there is no appeal, the dictum of an ignorant or pre·
sumptuous Grand l\faster (and both those qnalities have sometimes appeareu) should
override the better sense and better judgment of the entire assemblage whose chief
he unfortunately chanced to be. We recommend to our esteemed brother of Vermont, and others who may feel any interest in this subject, again to rend what we
wrote regarding it in 1858; and will leave it to themselves to judge whether a reverence for ancient customs, founded upon no better reason than that they ai·e ancient,
should outweigh every consideration of common sense and practical utility. Bro.
BcTLER dfaapprov~s, as we have done, of the regulation of Indiana relative to the
trial of Grand Masters; and he has rendered himself liable to be snubbed, as we have
been, for laughing a little at the " magnificent camp-meeting" project of the Grand
Master of Kansas. He entertains the same opinions as ourselves in regard to the so
called" right" to visit.:....cousidering the privilege neither" inherent" nor" absolute,"
but subject to such restrictions as circumstances and the exercise of a sound discretion may upon occasion indicate. He does not favor the Maine proposition for the
establishment of a General Grand Lodge; and is opposed, as, with three or four ex-

ADDRESS
" 1b the Most Worshipful Grand Masters and Grand Lodges of Ancient, Free and Accipted Masons on the Continent of North America:
"FRATERNAL SALUTATIONS: By the action of a Convention of Grand Lodges, begun
and holden in the city of Chicago, lllinois, the thirteenth day of September, 1859, in
response to a circular issued by the Grand Lodge of Maine, bearing date May, 1857,
it is made the duty, as it is the pleasure, of the undersigned, to address you and invite
your early and earnest attention to the proceedings of the said Convention; asking
that you will, after due consideration, take such action thereon as, in your wisdom,
the interests of your distinguished Grand Body and the interest• of Craft Masonry
seem to require.
" The proceedings of the Convention, which form a part of this circular, so fully
define the objects of the organization, as to leave little for this Committee to say by
way of explanation. The Articles of the Association, in their most essential features,
have been before the Grand Lodges of the country for nearly a year, in the proceed·
ings of the Grand Lodge of Minnesota, by her M.-.w... Grand Master, in response to
the circular from Maine. A careful comparison of those Articles with these now
submitted for your consideration, will show the truth of our assertion, that they have
been subjected to a patient and searching review, by five of our number, as well as
the careful scrutiny of a very large Convention, representing nearly all the Grand
Lodges of the United States, to which the largest liberty was allowed for criticism
and amendment. We certify you that the articles agreed upon, and the course pursued i_n their adoption, give ample assurance of our desire to guard the rights, dignity

for some time to come, he should abandon the pen and desk. The fraction of a re·
port now offered will exhibit abundant indications that this year its author was pot
fit for the task assigned him; and he begs to be excused, for the coming year at le'ast,
from further service on the Committee of Correspondence.

To the M:. JV:. Grand Lodge of' California : The undersigned, Trnstees of the Masonic Hall Fund, submit the following report:
At the last Annual Communication we reported that the Trnstees had been compelled to prosecute to foreclosure the mortgage taken to secure the loan ma~e by
the Trustees in 1857; and that, at the sale, a portion of the property had been bidden
in by ns. Not having been able to dispose of that property, it st~ll remains the property of the ~'und. We have, however, since our last report, received rents t~erefrom
to the amount of two hurn)red and fifty-five dollars and forty cents -the items of
which are contained in the detailed cash account of the Trnstees, accompanying this
report.
The two thousand dollar loan reported last year still continues. Having been
made so that the interest would compound, and being considered perfectly secure, it
has not been deemed advisable to insist upon any payments being made upon it.
The five hundred dollar loan reported last year, has been paid with the interest
thereon in full, as will be seen by reference to the cash account herewith.
We made during the past year one loan of one thousand dollars, which, with the
interest in full thereon, has been repaid, as can be seen from our cash account.
We have also received from Bro. A. MAHTIN, Grand Treasurer, his due bill for one
hundred and seventy-nine dollars and sixty cents, for interest on the amount of the
order of the Grand Secretary on him for two thousand dollars, dated September, 12,
1859, which amount of two thousand dollars we also received from him upon the
order of the Grand Secretary, as will be seen by the items of our cash account.
The cash account accompanying this report contains a detailed statement of each
item of receipts and disbursements, and shows a balance in the hands of the Trustees of

Bro. HENRY H. HAR1'LEY, from the special committee to whom was
referred at the last Annual Communication, the donation of certain lands
by Bro. A. M. WrnN, presented the following report: -

To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of' California:Your committee, to whom was referred the duty of reporting upon the title, value,
and condition of certain lands, heretofore donated by Bro. A. 1.f. WINN to this Grand
Lodge, represent as follows:That on the 29th of September, 1852, Bro. A. M. WJN~ executed to this Grand
Lodge a deed of a certain square or tract of land, of about twelve acres, in a town
then laid off by him adjoining the town of Suttcrville, in Sacramento county, and
called" Jerusalem"; that said town, like many others which sprang into being in the
early days of California, had an existence only on the map of the Civil Engineer who
traced its streets, avenues, public squares, &c., so that in speaking of it your committee can emphatically say "the grass grows in its streets and.highways"; and that
said land was granted to this Grand body on condition that it should, within ten years
from the date of the donation, erect upon said property a Masonic College, thus leaving this body but little over two yearH to comply with the condition.
The title to the property we believe to have been originally vested in JoHN A.
8UTTE!t, and within the lines of a grant from the Mexican government, as claimed by
him. But in the recent survey of said BUTTER'S grant, made by the Surveyor General
of California, the lines of said grant have been changed, and the entire tract of land
upon which the city of "Jerusalem" was located has been excluded; 11nd it is highly
probable that said grant will be finally located according to the calls of the said last
mentioned survey. Should this be the case, the conveyance will be entirely valueless,
as the grantor to this Grand body never having been in possession of said tract of
land, or claiming through any other source than the SoTTElt title, if that title be not
extended over it, possession thereof never can be obtained, as it is now held and
occupied by settlers claiming the lands as part of the public domain of the United
States.
·
A contingency might hereafter arise through which the property may be reduced
to possession by this Grand Lodge, but that contingency is so remote that your committee cannot recommend the expenditure of any funds, or the waste of any time or
0

All which is respectfully submitted.
HENRY HARE HARTJ,EY' Chairman.

Bro. ALEX. G. ABELL, from a special committee appointed at the last
Annual Communication, presented the following report:On Finances : ............................. .

To the -111:. W.-. Grand Lodge of California :

Your committee, to whom, at the last Annual Communication, was referred the
uniform code of by-laws for subordinates, heretofore recommended by this Grand
Lodge," for such revision as shall cause them to conform to the provisions of the
new Constitution," report that the duty assigned them has been performed.
In returning the form submitted, with the few corrections which were required,
your committee emMaee the occasion to express the opinion that it is almost as im·
portant that there shonld be similarity in the by-laws of the Lodges of a jurisdiction,
as that there should be uniformity in their work. Great convenience would certainly
be the result, were such a proposition carried into effect ; much Jess expense would
be incurred by the Lodges in their printing; and the committees of the Grand Lodge
would be relieved from a great portion of the annual and annoying labor of examining piles of regulations, as diverse in their length, law, and lack of judgment, as are
the experiences in other societies of the enterprising young Masons by whom they
are generally prepared. Our present Constitution provides for almost every conceivable case which can occur in a Lodge, and there is no necessity for re-writing it
in the form of by-laws. The few brief and simple rules which are here presented
are deemed amply sufficient for all the purposes required ; and your committee rec·
ommend the adoption of the following resolution : Resolved, That the by-laws for the government of subordinate Lodges, now submitted, are approved and adopted by tMs Grand Lodge; and that, from and after the
close of this Communication, they are declared to be the by·laws of each and every
Lodge now existing, or which may hereafter be established within this jurisdiction.
All which is respectfully submitted.
AI.EX. G. ABEJ.J,,

RECTOR E. COLE,

was doubtless intended to warn Bro. HENNING of his duty towards Bro. HARRIS, and
this sentence was much better calculated to obtain justice for Bro. HARRIS, tban a
more severe one. The J,odge should compel a submission of the matter in dispute,
and if by the award made, Bro. HENNING should be found In arrears or indebted to
Bro. HARRIS, under the circumstances set forth in the charge and evidence, and
should refuse to make restitution, he ought to be severely dealt with. Taking this
view of the case, and trusting that the course indicated may accomplish the ends of
justice, your committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution: Reso/1Jed, That the appeal of A. P. HARRIS in the matter of the trial, conviction,

Bro. JAs. L. ENGLISH, from the Committee on Grievances, presented
the following report:To the M:. W.·. Grand Lodge of California :-

Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. ROBERT McCoy from
the proceedings in a trial which resulted in the acquittal of Bro. BETHEL COOPWOOD,
by Unity Lodge, No. 130, have had the same under consideration. The charge was
disobedience of a summons, and the commissioners decided that the summons to Bro.
CooPwooD to appear" was not a proper summons in accordance with the edicts of
the Grand Lodge," and adjudged "the accused not guilty of disobeying a due summons." The defence to the charge appears to have been based upon the fact that
the Lodge did not order the summons to he issued. Your committee consider it intlisputable that a Master has power to issue a summons whenever the business of the
.Lodge requires it, without the order of the Lodge ; and that a brother receiving such
a summons has no right to question its legality and refuse t'o obey it. To admit this
right would be to destroy its efficiency. The commissioners therefore erred in their
finding, and your committee recommencl the adoption of the following resolution :Resolved, That the action of Unity Lodge, N o.130, in the case of BETHEL COOPWOOD,
be reversed and set aside, and that the case be remanded for a new trial.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Grand Lodge of OaJifornia :Your committee, to whom was referred the communication from the Secretary of
Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21, have read the same with much interest, and respectfully re·
port, that the peculiar position of that Lodge, in their opinion, requires special con·
sideration ou the part of tllis Grand Lodge. Its distant and comparatively isolated
location de bars it from receiving any of those privileges and advantages which result
from thiit ready fraternal intercourse and constant friendly communion with which
other Lodges are favored in this)urisdiction. Hawaiian Lodge has not been one of
those Masonic experiments which, we regret to say, are often attempted, and which,
by their failure to disseminate the true principles of our Order, are discreditable to
the Fraternity. On the contrary, it has been, and still is, a beacon-light which re.
fleets across an ocean on either side, those brilliant characteristics which we claim as
our most ennobling attributes; and, although beyond the reach of those instructions
which the Grand Lodge, through its lecturers, has at times imparted to its other sub·
ordinates, and oppressed by the weighty calls upon the liberal charity of its mem·
bers to which its peculiar position constantly subjects it, it has ever given evidence
of having performed all its duties well, and stands upon our record as a bright ex·
ampler of the self-existent ability of Masonry.
Your committee believe that too much consideration ca.n not be exhibited by the
Grand Lodge towards its ocean subordinate ; and that the small pecuniary contribu·
tion which it is our right to demand, it would, under all the circumstances of this case,
ill comport with our justice and dignity to receive. Your committee therefore rec·
ommend the adoption of the following resolution :Resolved, That the dues of Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21, for the year ending March
1st, 1860, be remitted, and that the amount already paid by that Lodge for such
;Jues, be refunded by the Grand Secretary.
All which is respectfully submitted.
CHARI.ES MARSH,
WM. A. JANUARY,
CHARI.ES L. WIGGIN,
ANDREW C. KEAN,

Bro. GILBERT R CLAIBORYE, from the special committee upon the communication relative to a North American Congress, presented the following
report:To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of Calij'urnia :-

The special committee to whom was referred the proceedings of the Masonic Con·
vention, held at Chicago, in the month of September last, for the purpose of organ·
izing " A North American Masonic Congress," have carefully considered the Articles
of Association and the address of the committee inviting this Grand Lodge, among
others, to become a member of that body, and report: that this Grand Lodge having
already proclaimed itself a supreme Masonic power and authority, any action which
tends, however remotely, to impair its supremacy, should be jealously avoided, as
dangerous to its dignity and independence. They believe that by adopting the Arti·
cles of the Association the effect would be 11 tendency to trammel and circumscribe this
body in its deliberations and action; and, while they commend a spirit which seems
to labor to promote the progress of the Order and increase its prosperity, they deem
it prudent and wise that this Grand Lodge should remain as it is, entirely independent
of all other Masonic bodies, legislfl.tive, judicial, or advisory, in all things save those
courtesies and kind offices which become Masonic committees as well as individuals.

360

[May 11,

Your committee therefore recommend that the Grand Lodge do not a<lopt the
Articles of Association of said Congress.
All which is respectfully submitte<l.
GILBERT ll. CLAIBORNE,

To the .M.·. W. ·. Grand Lodge of California; Your committee, to whom was referred a resolution proposing to donate the fund~
and property formerly belonging to the late San Francisco Lodge, No. 'i, to Pacific
and Crockett Lodges, lately organized in the city of San Prancisco, respectfully beg
leave to report: that after carefully considering all the circumstimces of' the case,
they find that the petitioners for the Dispensations to the two Lodges last named were
members of San Francisco Lodge, No. 7, at the time of the revocation of its cliarter.
The petitioners for the establishment of Pacific Lodge (thirty-three in number,) were
granted a Dispensation at the last Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge ; tho><c
for the establishment of CrockPtt Lodge (thirteen in number,) were granted a Dispensation by t11e .;.VI.·. W.·. Grand Master on the eighteenth day of August, 1859; and for both

a difference of opinion between tlie delegates from the two J.odgc:; as to the amount

this donation. 'rhe representatives of Pacific Lodge insist npon a pro rata distribn·
