while those of CrockPtt Lodge do not ask for the donation at all, but insist that they
are entitled to an equal amount with Pacific Lodge, should the funds of San Fran·
cisco Lodge be donated as requested io this resolution.
There wer'" sixty·nine members borne upon the roll of San Francisco Lodge at the
date of its last annual return, which leaves one third of its former members not con·
nected with either of the Lodges herein named ; and, for augl1t your committee know,
these maY form themselves into a new Lodge, or affiliate with some other Lodge, and
with the ~ame degree of propriety may ask for their share of the funds of the extinct
Lodge. Therefore, in the opiniQn of your committee, equal and exact justice to all
the members of the late San Ji'rancisco I,odge would not be attained by tl1e passage
of the resolution submitted for their consideration. They are of the opinion that
upon the surrender or forfeiture of the charter of a Lodge, all its effects become the
property of the Grand Lodge, by operation of the Constitution; an~ they deem i~ h'.·
expedient for this Grand Lodge to make Yolnntary donations from its funds to mdt·
vitlual Lodges.
Your committee therefore return the resolution, with the recommendation that it
be not adopted.

Bao. WILLIAM S. WELLS, from the special committee to whom was referred the memorial of 0. C. OsnoRNE, praying a restoration to the rights
and privileges of Masonry, presented the following report:To the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of California:-

Your committee, to whom was referred the petition of O. C. OSBORNE, have had the
same under consideration, and beg leave to report; that the petitioner was expelled
by the late San Franei8co Lodge, No. 7; on the twentieth day of February, 1856, upon
a charge of having converted to his own use the funds of the Lodge, while Treasurer
thereof, and of being a defaulter for the same ; that he appealed from the sentence,
and that his appeal was acted upon by the Grand Lodge at its annual Communication
in May, 1856, upon his own statement-no transcript or record of proceedings having
been sent up.
The Committee on Grievances of that year reported that, after patient examination
of the statement of the appellant, they could find nothing which in their opinion
would warrant the Grand Lodge in remandlng the case to San Francil!co Lodge, for a
new trial, and recommended a dismissal of tl1e appeal and the confirmation of the
sentence. This report was concurred in by the Grand J,odge, as will be seen in the
proceedings of that year, Vol. II, p. 327.
Your committee are unable to find in the memorial under consideration any thing
tending to impeach the justice of the sentence passed by San Francisco J,odge, or
the action of the Grand J,odge thereupon. On the contrary, the memorial fully confirms the previous action in the case, and there appears nothing either in the petition
or the records of the Grand Lodge to warrant the reversal or modification of the
sentence heretofore pronounced.
But the Grand Lodge is asked to take a charitable view of tbe case, and, permit·
ting the petitioner to give an evidence of his indebtedness to the Lodge, with reason·
able use for the money, to restore him to full fellowship with the Fraternity.
Without assuming to direct the action of the Grand J,odge upon charitable subjects, your committee deem it proper to say that, in their opinion, just,ice to the
Fraternity requires that the memorial should not be entertained until full restitution
of the amount taken, with interest, be made to the Grand Lodge, as the successor of
San Francisco I.odgc, No. 7, or good and sufficient reasons be shown why the debt,
or any part of it, should be forgiven. Sufficient assurance also should be given that
the character and conduct of the petitioner arc such as to guarantee the Fraternity
against further injury from the same source. The mere " acknowledgment of in·
debtedness" is a poor substitute for the restitution that shonld be made ; and no cir·
cumstances are set forth in the memorial that would justify a remission of the debt.
Your committee have information that since 1856, the petitioner resided for a year or
two in this jurisdiction, and was at one time in such circumstances that he might
have restored to the J.odge the amount so taken had he been disposed so to do.
Your committee, therefore, deeming lt inexpedient, for the reasons herein given,
to entertain the memorial of o. C. OsBORN.E, recommend that he have leave to withdraw the same.

Bro. H. F. WILLIAMS, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented
the following report:-

To the M.'. W.-. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom wa~ referred the appeal of JOHNS. WII.LIAMS from the
trial and acquittal of' W.J:LLIAM MILLING, by California Lodge, No. 1, have had the
same under consideration. A number of points have been made upon the argument
of the appeal, which we will dispose of in the reverse order of their presentation.
Fierst-It is objected that tile commi>!sioners disregarded the positive proof on the
charge of slander. It hi trne that there is positive proof in the record to sustain the
charge ; but it appears to be equally true that this testimony was not credited by the
commissioners. Those who hear the testimony of witnesses have peculiar opportunities of judging of their credibility, and this it is their province to determine ; and
when it appears that positive proof to a point is not credited by those who tried the
case, an appellate tribunal, which has not the witnesses before it, will never decide
that the triers should have believed the witnesses, and on such a ground reverse 11
finding. We say then that there is no error here.
Second-That the commissioners refused to grant the accuser a reasonable time to
procure his testimony. Prom the admitted facts of the case, we believe that the accused had ample time to procure his testimony, had he used reasonable diligence in
obtaining it. The Grand Lodge having decided that an acquittal is no bar to a second
trial for the same offense, the accuser has the privilege of producing his testimony by
fl ling new charges.
Third-That the substance only of the testimony was taken down, and not the
words of the witnesses. There is no doubt but that the proper rule for taking testimony is to take the words of the witness, and not the substance of what he says,
as understood by those engaged in taking it. There is always room for construe·
tion of testimony, and that construction should always be given by those who are to
pass upon it, arid not by those who commit it to writing. But in the present case, the
appellant has sustained no injury in the premises, not only because there is no material dilference between the evidence in the record and the notes of the evidence as
taken and furnished by the couneel of the accuser, but because the witnesses themselves were not believed by the commissioner8.
Fourth-That the commissioners refused to require the accused to answer the
eharge. The appellant appears to think that where the Constitution provides that the
accused shall be summoned "to appear and answer," it means that the accused shall
appear and plead to the charge; but we un<lersfamd the word " answer" to signify
that he shall appear and "face" the charge, in which sense the word is frequently
used. We see nothing in the Constitution which wonld require the technical construction to be given to the word for which the applicant contends. The record show~,
too, that before the conclusion of the trial the accused was called on by the commis.
sioners to re~pond specifically to each charge and specification, and that he did so
respond.
·
Fifth-'rhat the coimnissioners who were charged \Jy the uccuser with bias at the
first meeting of the commlssioncro, refused to withdraw from the commission. It is
too late to challenge the commisoionm·s after they have assembled for trial. Were
snch a rule to be aclmltted, there might never be a trial under the present system. It
iK the dnty of the members of the Lodge who desire an impartial trial to be had, to
attend at the special meetings of the Lodge, and see that no biased commissioner is
elected; and sl10uld such an one be chosen, to have him !set aside, and an impartia I
one substituted.

[May 11,

Si:tth-That the accused was presQnt in the Lodge .during the election of the com·

missioners. The accused, being a member of the Lodge in good standing, had a right
to be present. It was also impqrtant to him that he should be there, to see that impartial commissioners were selected.
Seventh-That the members of the J,odge were not duly notified to attend the
special meeting to elect commissioners. It is admitted that the notice given was an
announcement of the special meeting at the previous'"meeting, and a publication of'
a notice of the special meeting in the newspapers. The CQllstitusion of this Grand
Lodge provides that, npon the presentation of charges, it shall be the duty of the
Master, "by due notification," to call a special meeting of his Lodge for the election
of commissioners. A "notijiraticm" is defined by the Constitution to be " a call issued
by the Secretary, by order of the Lodge or Master, or by other competent authority,
as hereinbefore provided, to attend for some specific purpose at the time and place
therein indicated." We find that a "summons" is defined by the Constitution to be
"an imperative order issued by the Master 01' by other competent authority, as hcreinbefore provided, to appear at such time and place as may therein be designated.''
Stripping these two definitions of all verbiage unnecessary to a determination of the
point now under consideration, we find that a notification is " a call issued by the
Secretary to attend at the time and place therein indicated"; while a summons is
" an imperative order issued by the Master to appear at said time and place, as may
therein be designated." Nothing whatever is said as to the mode of service of either,
bnt as the definition of the two are so very similar, varying only sufficiently to indi·
cate to the brethren served the difference between the two, we think there is no
doubt but that a notification and a summons should be served in a similar manner ;
for if this was not intended, or if any mode of notification could be adopted which a
Lodge might see proper to select, why did this Grand Lodge define what a notification is? We are therefore of the opinion that a notification shonld be served in the
same manner as a summons. Now, would any one suppose for a moment, that the
announcement of the Master at a stated meeting, that an .the members of the Lodge
were summoned to appear at a certain time, would be a service of the snmmons upon
all the members of the Lodge, or would the publication of a summons in the newspapers be so regarded? Unquestionably not, How then could such announcement or
publication be considered due notification? In the opinion of your committee it
cannot be, as this Grand J,,odge has decided that in a case of charges preferred, it is
the duty of the Master to see that every member of his Lodge, who can possibly be
notified of' the meeting, is notified in duii season. The notification of the special
meeting to elect commissioners in this case, therefore, was not sufficient, and for this
reason we must annul the proceedings.
We see that which we deem an error in the record, which was not adverted to by
any one upon the argnment of the appeal. A Fellow Craft was admitted to testily
upon his honor as a Mason; this was wrong, as none but Master Masons should be
vermitted so to testify- all others should be sworn.
Your committee th.eiefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resolved, That the'''~ction of California Lodge, No. 1, in the case of WILLIAM
MILLI:NG, be reversed and set aside, and that the case be remanded for further pro·
ceedings.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Bro. H. F. 'VILLIAMS, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented
the following reports :
To the M .-• W.·. Grand Lodge of California:Your committee, to whom was referred the memorial from Los Angeles Lodge,
No. 42, presented by Bro. JOHN G. DOWNEY, expressing the desire of that J,odge that
it be permitted to restore Mr. W.W. Rt:BOTTO:M to membership therein, and that a
lecturer be appointed to visit that and other of the southern Lodges, l1ave had the
~arue under consideration, and report as follows:
The particnlars of tl1e case of Mr. Rt:BOTTOY are so familiar to the Grand Lodge,
that they need not be here repeated. A report from this committee, presented at the
last Annual Communication, ltnd concurred in by the Grand J,odge, expressed its
views of the injustice which, in its belief, had probably been done to him by the action
of one of the subordinates of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas, and it.s commendation
of the prompt and satisfactory manner in which Los Angeles Lodge, No. 42, bad vindicated itself from the charge of unmasonic conduct which had been brought against
it. Those views your committee still entertain, and if they had felt any doubt before,
as to the character of Mr. RUBOTTOM, the strong testimony in his favor contained in
the paper presented by Bro. DOWNEY, would entirely have dispelled it. "Mr. RuHOTTO.M, during his residence in this State," says he," l1as conducted himself with the
utmost propriety. There is no resident of Lo;; Angeles county more highly and justly
esteemed; and I sincerely desire that our Lodge may be empowered to admit him to
membership." Such words from the Governor of California, as high in the esteem of
his brethren and fellow citizens as he is in official position, should have no common
weight; and testimony like this, when superadded to all which has been received be·
fore, would determine your committee at once to recommend a compliance with the
wish of Los Angeles Lodge, were they not prevented hy the consideration thatit might

1860.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

373

be deemed an act of discourtesy to the Grand Lodge of .Arkansas. It is true that the
p·apers in t!J,is case were transmitted to the Grand Secretary of that State long before
the last .Annual Uomnnmication of that body-that six months have now elapsed
since that Communication-and that no reply has been thus far vouchsafed to us.
Yet there may be some good reason for the delay, and we should not hurriedly do a
thing, however intrinsically just it may be deemed, which might well be considered
by our esteemed contemporary of Arkansas, as not only discourteous, but violative
of one of the most important of Masonic usages. There is no better established custom in the Masonry of the United States, than that the Lodge, (or the Grand Lodge
under whose jurisdiction such Lodge exists) which expels or suspends a Mason,
should alone have the right to restore him; and your com.nittee, however much they
sympathize with Mr. RUDOTTO::ll and our brethren of Los Angeles, would deeply regret
to see the Grand Lodge of California the first to overleap a rule so salutary. They
can onlyrecommenil, therefore, that the Grand Secretary be. instructed again to direct
the attention of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas to this subject, and that no further
action be taken thereupon until our next .Annual Communication.
In regard to the appointment of a lecturer, as suggested in the memorial as there
iH now no authorized Grand Lecturer for this jurisdiction, your committ~e feel at
liberty only to suggest that the Grand Master, if he can procure the services of some
brother well skilled in the work prescribed by this Grand Lodge, should authorize
him to act in the capacity requested.
All which is respectfully submitted.
H. I<'. WILLIAMS,

To the M.-. W.·: Grand Lodge of California : Your committee, to whom were referred certain papers relative to CHARLES HUNT

In regard to the first case, it appears that Mr. HUNT has, during five years past,
been borne upon tlie roll of Petaluma Lodge, No. 77, as one of its members, and that
information has heen lately received that in the year 18.52 he was expelled by Eagle
Lodge, No. 12, at Keokuk, in the State of Iowa, for non-payment of dues. .Although
expulsion fo~ such a cause is a harsher penalty than our own laws permit, it was
doubtless authorized by the Grand I,odge under whose Jurisdiction it was inflicted·
and it is therefore to !Je respected liy this Grand Lodge and its subordinates. Yon;
committee are convinced that Petaluma Lodge, No. 77, knew not the position of Mr.
HuNT when he was a:(liliated, and they therefore llttach no blame to the J,odge for his
admission, as at that time the presentation of a <limit was not, as now, imperatively
required.
In regard to t.he seconil case, it appears that }fr. COMSTOCK has, during four years
past, been borne upon the roll of Humboldt Lodge, No. 79, as one of its members, and that official information has been received hy the Graml Secretary that in

the position occupied by Mr. COMSTOCK, until recently informed by the Grand Secre·
tary, anrl it is due to it to say that he was at once excluded upon receipt of that information. Your committee recommend the adoption of the following resolution:-

On motion of Bro. JEssE MoRRII.L, the following report from the Committee on Finances, presented yesterday, was taken from the table.
To the M.·. W.-. Grand Lodge of California : Your committee, to whom was referred the report of the Trustees of the Masonic
Hall Fund, have carefully examined the same, and beg leave to submit the following:
They believe the moneys belonging to the fund to have been managed carefully
and with the best pecuniary ability possible, taking into consideration the precariouR
nature of ~ecurities in California, and the uncertainty invariably attendant upon investments among a people so changeable and speculative. :N" o loss has been sustained, but on the C!intrary, the fund has received a considerable increa.se. But your
committee feel it their duty to suggest to the Grand Lodge the propriety of obtaining
till investment for this fund, which would be positive and certain in its character,
not subject to the contingencies which follow the ordinary loaning of money here,
and yet, likely to alford a fair and reasonable rate of interest.
'.!.'hey are informed that such an opportunity is now presented. The brethren of
the city of San :Franci>co have formed an association for tl1e purpose of erecting an
edifice to be dernted to the uses of Masonry, which will be alike creditable to the·
Order and to the State. This association is controlled entirely by Masons, is incorpo·
rated under our State laws, and has at this time invested in the enterprise ovar sixty
thousand dollars of the one hundred thousand v:hich form its capital stock; and, af·

[May 12,

Proceedings of the

ter a careful consideration-of the matter, your committee have concluded to recommend to the Grand Lodge that the usual amount to be appropriated at this Communication, together with the entire Ma.sonic Hall Fnnd, be invested in the stock of "The
Masonic Hall Association of the City of San Francisco.'' Your committee express
their approbation of the business-like manner in which the Trustees have performed
the somewhat onerous duties imposed upon them, suggest that they are entitled to
the highest commendation on the part of the Grand Lodge, and recommend the following resolution for adoption : Resolved, That the moneys now in the hands of the 'frustces of the Masonic Hall
Fund, and being a portion of that fund, together with such amount as shall be appropriated at this Communication for an addition to that fund, be invested in the stock
of the" Masonic Hall Association of the City of San Francisco"; that all the moneyH
belonging to said fund, now out ·on loan, be called in at th.e earliest date possible,
and be also invested in said stock; and that such other property as belongs to that
fund, be disposed of as soon as practicable, and be invested in the same manner.
All whirh is respectfully submitted.

CHARLES MARSH,

DECISIONS BY THE GRAND MASTER.

____

......,._________...._._

In reply to sundry questions propounded during this Communication, the Grand
Master gave the following decisions, viz. : 1. A :Mason may make application for affiliation as often as it may please him so
to do. The rejection of his petition for that purpose by a Lodge, simply implies that
that particular Masonic family, or some one or more of its members, has objection to
the immediate association, but it does not prevent'him from applying for membership
to any other Lodge. or to the same one, at any time thereafter.
2. Suspension for non-payment of dues is absolute suspension. The disabilities
which it involves under onr laws, are the same as if the penalty had beeu incurred by
unmasonic conduct. In fact, such is really the misdemeanor which has induced the
punishment, as a violation of the by-law>i of a Lodge (all which require the payment
of certain quarterly or monthly dues) is eminently unmasonic. The only dilference
which our Constitution makes between suspension for (so called) unmasonic conduct,
and suspension for non-payment of dues, is, that in the first case, it requires the votes
of two-thirds of the Lodge of which the delinquent was a member, to effect his resto·
ration, while in the second, he may r(\store himself by payment of his arrearages.
3. It is not necessary that a Mason should be a member of the Lodge nearest his
place of residence. lie may hold membership, or apply for it, wherever it shall
please him. It is certainly better that he should be a member of the Lodge within
whose jurisdiction he resides, but I know of no law which requires it; and to be a
member, in good standing, in any regular Lodge, is to be in good standu;g everywhere.
4. In cases of trial, a majority of the Commissioners, elected or appointed, may
proceed with the business committed to them. The Constitution does not say thus
much in terms, but it does by inference, as it declares that" the judgment of a
majority of the Commissioners shall be taken as the decision of the whole." To rule
otherwise would be to defeat the justice sought for in the regulations upon this subject, as it would probably not often happen that all the Commissioners named would
be in attendance during the whole period given for a trial under onr Constitution.
The vote npon the finding and the sentence should be by ballot, and a majority of
all the Commissioners is requisite for judgment.
5. The Master of a Lodge has absolute control within his Lodge. Our ritual pre·
scribes that none shall enter without his permission, and he may refuse admission to
any at his discretion. He may even cause a member of his Lodge to be exclnded or
removed, but he must recollect that there should be strong cause for the exercise of
such an act of authority, and that the Constitution provides a remedy for those who
. may be aggrieved by the abuse of the power which his station temporarily gives him.
6. The position occupied by non-affiliated Masons in this State is plainly defined
in the Constitution. In Sec. 1, Art. II, Part V, of that instrument it is declared that
"it is the duty of every Master Mason to be a member of some Lodge ; and every
one who, having resided six months within the jurisdiction of a Lodge, shall refuse or
neglect to make application so to be, or wbo shall not have regularly contributed to
such Lodge aa amount equivalent to its regular dues, while able so to do, shall be
deemed unworthy of Masonic consideration, and shall not be entitled to, or be the
recipient of, any of the rights, privileges, or charities of the Order." Tl!is is literally
the language of suspension, and, under this law, every non-affiliated Mason, coming
within its purview, is absolutely suspended, until by compliance with either of the
alternatives which it provides, he shall choose to free himself from the disability.

THE UNIFORM CODE OF BY-LAWS
FOR THE SUBORDINATE LODGES OF THIS JURISDICTION,
As Revised and Recommended by the Grand Lodge, in May, 1860.

ARTICLE I.
OF NAME AND OFFICERS.
SECTION I. 'l'his Lodge shall be known by the name of. ................. Lodge,
No ..... ., of ~'ree and Accepted Masons; and its officers shall consist of a Master, a
Senior Warden, a Junior Warden, a 'freasurer, a Secretary, a Senior Deacon, a Junior Deacon, a Marshal, two Stewards, a Tyler, and such other officers as the Lodge
may deem proper to appoint.
ARTICLE II.
OF ELECTIONS AND APPOINTMENTS,
SECTION 1. The Master, the Senior and Junior Wardens, the Treasurer, and the
Secretary shall be elected by ballot, in conformity with Section 1, Article I, Part IV,
of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge. The other officers shall be appointed by the
Master, except the Junior Deacon, who may be appointed by the Senior Warden.
ARTICLE III.
01' MEETINGS OF THE LODGE.

SECTION 1. The stated meetings of this Lodge shall be holden on the ............ .
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .in each month.
SEc. 2. Special meetings may be called from time to time, as the Lodge, or the
presiding officer thereof, may direct.
ARTICLE IV.
OF INITIATION AND MEMBERSHIP.
SECTION 1. All petitions for initiation or affiliation must be signed by the petitioner,
and be recommended by two members of the Lodge. Every such petition shall be
referred to a committee of three, whose duty it shall be to report thereon at the next
stated meeting, (unless further time be granted,) when the applicant maybe balloted
for, and received or rejected, or the ballot may be postponed until the ensuing stated
meeting, as the Lodge may determine.
SEC. 2. If any applicant, elected to receive the degrees in this Lodge, does not
come forward to be initiated within three months thereafter, the fee shall be forfeited, unless the Lodge shall otherwise direct.
SEC. 3. Every person raised to the degree of Master Mason in, or elected a member of this Lodge, shall sign the By-Laws thereof.

ARTICLE V.
OF THE TREASURER.
SECTION 1. The Treasurer shall receive all moneys from the Secretary ; shall keep
an accurate and just account thereof; and shall pay the same out only upon an order
duly signed by the Master, and countersigned by the Secretary. He shall, at the
stated meetings in June and December of eac11 year, submit a report in full of the
monetary transactions of the I,odge. The Lodge may also, at any time when considered necessary, cause him to present an account of his receipts and disbursements,
and the amount of funds on hand.
SEC. 2. He shall, if required by the Lodge, execute a good and sufficient bond to
the Master, for the faithful performance of liis duties.
ARTICLE VI.
OF THE SECRETARY.
SECTION 1. The Secretary shall keep a faithful record of all proceedings proper to
be written ; shall transmit a copy of the same to the Grand Lodge, when required ;
shall keep a separate account for each memoer of the Lodge ; shall report at the
stated meetings in June and December the amounts due by each; shall receive all
moneys due the I,odge, and pay the same to the Treasurer; and shall perform all
such other duties as may properly appertain to his office.
SEc. 2. He shall receive such comp~psation for his services, as the Lodge may direct.
ARTICLE VII •.
OF THE TYLER.
SECTION 1. The Tyler, in addition to the necessary duties of his office, shall serve
all notices and summonses, and perform such other services as may be required of
him by the J,odge.
SEc. 2. He shall receive such compensation for his serviceA, as the Lodge may dL
rect.

And the Grand Lodge of California was opened in ~mpl.t ,form, with

The Grand 1\-laster announced that the Grand Lodge had been convened
for the purpose of laying the Corner Stone of the Masonic Temple now
being erected by the Masonic Hall Association of the City of San Francisco,
in consonance with the invitation of that Association, presented and
accepted at the late Annual Communication ; and, after a brief address
appropriate to the occasion, directed the Grand Lodge to be called off for
the purpose of fo'rming a procession to proceed to the place of ceremony.
The Grand Chapter of Royal Arch Masons of the State of Californiu,
then convened in the lower Masonic Hall in accordance with a similar
invitation from the Masonic Hall Association to be present at the ceremonies, having notified the Grand Marshal of its readiness to proceed; and

The Fraternity thus formed, numbering over one thousand, traversed
several of the principal streets of the city, and, upon arriving at the site
of the new Ten1ple, on the corner of Montgomery and Post Streets, the
bead of the procession halted opposite a triumphal arch, which had been
erected at the entrance to the platforms which covered the eastern portion
of the baBement walls. The Knights Templar dismounted, and arranged
themselves within to receive the Grand Lodge. The lines were opened to
the right and left, under the direction of the Grand Marshal; and the
Grand Master, preceded by two Stewards and the Grand Sword Bearer, and
followed by the Grand Lodge, the Grand Chapter, and the remainder of the
procession in inversed order, passed through to the raised platform erected
near the north-east corner of the building, upon which seats had been prepared for the officers and members of the Grand Bodies, and the most distinguished of the invited guests. The Grand Master was seated in front
of th{l centre of the platform, immediately surrounded by the principal officers of the Grand Lodge. Upon a table before him were placed by their
several bearers the Holy Writings, the Book of Constitutions; the Golden
Vessel of Corn, the two Silver Vessels containing Wine and Oil, the three
large Lights, the five Orders of Architecture, and the. Working Tools. The

It is a source of heartfelt joy to all the Craft assembled here, to participate with
you in the inauguration of this glorious work. You do well to build this Temple, to
which the toil-worn craftsman shall turu with confidence, and find refresl1ment and

May symmetry and order rest upon each line and curve, and strength and beauty
characterize each arch and pillar, from base to cape-stone ; and may the grandeur of
its proportions attract tbe admiration and gladden the heart of every lover of order
and of progress.

cate fraternity and good will among men; and may it be completed by the craftsmen
in peace, love, and harmony-they suffering no contention among themselves except

The following eloquent oration was then delivered by the Grand Orator
for the day, Sir HENRY M. GRAY:BRETHREN :-Beneath the blue dome of this wide, unpillared firmament, a~d 1:nder
the magnificent roof of a temple "not made with hands," we are met m JOY!Ul
assemblage, upon a day sacred to the ancient memories of our Craft, to lay with
appropriate and impressive ceremonies the founda~ion-stone of a temple, henceforth
and forever to be sacredly dedicated to the mysteries and work of Masonry·
In due form and manner the corn, wine, and oil poured forth upon that stone, have
symbolized the great end and object of Masonic life; the swell. of joyous musi.c wl~
its exultant harmony, has awakened in our breasts the responsive ec.ho; the light m
a thousand earnest eyes, and the quickened throb of a thousand lovmg hearts, have

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

496

told how deeply this scene and this hour have impressed themselves upon our very
souls ; and, finally, the invocation of the blessing of Almighty God, to direct and
prosper this undertaking to its successful completion, has, while it humbly aclmow·
ledges our dependence upon His powerful aid, given us the trustful hope that His
paternal blessing shall be vouchsafed to us.
Brethren, the work is done! In the deep foundations of this structure you have
placed your memorial. For the first time on the western shores of this continent,
you have set up the pillars of your faith in enduring stone. In the generations yet to
come, who shall gaze with pride upon this noble pile, and who shall under its secure
shelter prosecute the glorious mission which Masonry has entrusted to their keeping,
your labors will not be forgotten. They will recall, with proud and glowing retrospects,
the memory of this day. They will pay due homage to the loyal faith, the loving
interest, and the deathless attachment which you held to the great work of Masonry,
and which prompted you, in the very infancy of our State, thus to lay broad and deep
the imperishable foundations of a Temple, which, while it shOuld be one of the most
conspicuous adornments of our city, should also serve as a perpetual record of that
faith which, in all ages and in all countries, has, in its" outward visible form," illustrated itself to the world in all the grand triumphs of architectural glory, us, in the
manifestations of its inner life, it has been the pioneer in the vanguard of civilization,
charity, peace, brotherly kindness, and good will to men. If ever the light burns dim
upon our altars, or the hearts of the faithful fail them "because of fear;" if the
doubter or the skeptic ask," The Fathers, where are they? "-then shall this Masonic
temple answer; "The same faith that animated their hearts still survives in their
descendants. This goodly Tabernacle, which the ancient craftsmen builded, yet
stands in its pristine strength and beauty, a sacred heritage to be sacredly guarded
and preserved by us and by those who shall come after us. So, evermore, shall the
faithful remembrance of our brethren yet to be, preserve our memory green.''
All creeds and faiths.have their festal occasions. The State has its days of patriotic jubilee, the Church its sea.sons of rejoicing. On commemorative days, due homage is paid to all who, in every rank and in every good work, have adorned the age
they illustrated. Thus religion, art, science, heroism, virtue, wherever their votaries
have ennobled life by grand achievements, have claimed the ready homage of the
world. They who have died on the bloody fields of battle for the liberties of their country, where thousands in the joyous rush of death go down-they who in the fires of martyrdom have yielded up their lives a sacrifice to principle-they who in toilsome solitude have worked out the great problems of science, and given language and interpretation to the mute voices of nature-they who with strong hands and pure ambi·
tions have guided the evolving destinies of nations--they who, as the apostles of divinest charity, have devoted life, substance, inlluence, all to the amelioration of human wrong or suffering, are ulike canonized in the world's great heart, and compel
the homage of the world's wide sympathy.
This ls our festal day, my brethren; to us, a day of joy in a two-fold sense. This
happy hour is witness of a ceremony of no small import to the future of Masonry in
this State and 011 this coast. We have come up together, with one accord, to aid in
the laying of the corner-stone of the first Masonic Temple erected within the limits
of our national confederation, on the westward slopes of the dividing mountains. For
a brief space we have forsaken our usual avocations; and from fields of waving grain,
from work-shops of daily toil, from the quiet retreats of scientific pursuits, from the
busy marts of' commerce, from the sacred chancels of religion, we have come with
" one heart, and one mind," to swell the pomp of this festive hour. Hallowed by our
prayers and benedictions, we have placed the token of our affection to Masonry in
the keeping of our mountain granite. Our loves, our hopes, our aspirations, we place
beside those memorials: as soon may the one perish as the others. Not until the solid
rock shall melt in the consuming fires of the final conllagration, shall die out in our

We speak of martyrdoms, and they are glorious. We speak of!ieroisms, and they
are glorious. How they stand out in the cloudy past, like landmarks in the life·
gloom, these martyrs for the good !-these heroes for the right! Some have sunk on
the battle-field ; some have watered the scaffold with their blood ; others have per·
ished in the agonies of fire. These have been of one race and language; those of
another. '.1.'his endured all things for one faith; that for another: but all, whatever
their nation, or sect, or lineage, were alike the warriors of humanity, and perished
that mankind might be free. The great and good of all eras form one great brother·
hood. Thank God for having thus linked distant ages together by the ties of a com·
mon sympathy. The great souls scattered along the highway of history, are bound
one to the other by an electric chain ; and thus the influence of heroic deeds thrills
from century. to century down the long avenue of Time.
This day, my brethren, is held in sacred commemoration of St. John the Baptist,
throughout the whole Masonic world. Every aspiration and prayer that ari~c~ 10-r!nv
from your own full hearts, is met in the silent and illimitable fields of air uy o. w ••• ._ ••
aspirations in every land and clime, from hearts as full and deep as yours.
.A.ll along the cloudy pathway of time our Craft have left their ever-enduring land·
marks. While yet an operative organization, spreading from land to land, in Lodges
of Labor, they have erected their mighty monuments, which, to this day, are the
wonder and the glory of the w.orld. The grand order and system which marked the
building of the first temple, followed them in the latter ages; and although in the erec·
tion of the vast creations of Masonic skill, the busy sounds of labor were heard on
every hand, as the grand arches and pinnacles and towers rose from their solid foun·
dations to the heavens, yet the same beautiful plan of work by which the magnificent
structure of the King of Israel
"Rose like an exhalation, witl:> the sound
Of dulcet symphonies, and voices sweet,"

governed the Craft in the building of those colossal triumphs of architectural genius,
which shall forever demand the admiration and worship of the human intellect.
Passing from this brief review of our subject, let us for a moment consider our
institution in its adaptation to the wants of humanity,; its fitness as the almoner of
the holiest charity; its laws and precepts as the embodiment, not only of the purest
morality, but presenting likewise a frame of government fitted for all conditions of
life, for all races of people, and for all states of society. It sprang into existence far
back in the distant ages, over whose history rests the pall of everlasting silence; it
gleamed out of that darkness as the light of history began to irradiate the gloom
only in dim and fabulous traditions ; it took organic shape and practical development
in the earliest days of the ancient Kings of Israel; and its culminating point was
reached in that perfect system of work and government which presided over the
~rection of that miraculous structure-that marble poem of consummate genius whose
lovely beauty, shining from the sacred mountain, gleamed to the remotest horizon
like a star.
Thus it has come down to us from the earliest times. Through all the changes of
empires, and amid all the revolutions of governments, it has preserved its existence.
The altar now stands where it stood in the days of the first Masters ; and the enkind·
led fires and the emblematic lights still shed their beams to illuminate the surrounding
darkness. It has outlived the Temple which its ancient Craftsmen builded; but the
same laws that held it in harmonious union then, alike preserve its unity and integrity
now. The forms of architectural beauty and design may have gone down in the dust

29

498

Special Oommunication of the

[June 25,

of the vanished ages, but the soul and spirit of the design, order and beauty, yet lingers in our Craft and hallows all its work.
From Praxitelean shapes, whose marble smiles
" Fill the hushed air with everlruiting love ; "

from towers and arches, mouldering among their mocking ivy ; from the solemn
cloisters of many an old cathedral; from the dim aisles of grand old woods, whose
mighty trees are evermore repeating
"Their old poetic legends to the winds;"
from the stupendous caves with all their sparry grots; and from the grand rock-invested gorges of the mountains, whose beetling walls might serve as the bastions of a
world, where the sublime Architect of the Universe has, in the play of His omnipotence, set those grand copies for human genius to imitate : from each and all, the
lesson falls with a deep significance on the Mason's heart. Architecture, its first great
operative application, compelled the recognition of the laws of unity and order.
From the study and contemplation of the great principles upon which the harmony
of the material universe depended, the transition was natural and easy to the recognition and adoption of those laws governing the life, conduct, character, and actions,
upon which alone, as npon a corner stone, could be erected the moral and spiritual
Temple of Masonry.
Neither the time nor the occasion demand from me an exposition of the tenets
and principles of the Craft. I may.however, be allowed for a brief moment to allude
to some of the excellences of our Order.
And first, its sublime equality. Its first prmciple is the recognition of the humanity of the man, and the acknowledgment of the fraternal ties that bind all men
together. Within its sacred enclosure there can be no rank or caste. The royal
ruler of a mighty realm; the mitred prelate; the soldier. bearing upon his body the
scars and trophies of a hundred fights ; the philosopher, whose keen vision has explored all the intricacies of natural or political wisdom; the soul of science that hath
sojourned among the stars or dived into the nethermost depths-are all alike. Brethren all-made so by the recognition of each individual humanity-and each an equal
scholar in the school of virtue. "Love one another" is written upon the door-posts,
and the word" Brother" embraces in its comprehensive dialect, all ranks, from the
Neophyte to the Supreme Master.
While prejudice alienates-while sect and nation, lineage and language, wealth
and power, set up evermore the barriers which keep men asunder-while political
distinctions and religious differences but deepen animosities and engender bitterness-Masonry presents a platform and a principle broad and firm enough for all the world
to rest upon in peace.
In the grand Choral Hymn of the noble Schiller, I find these lines, which only
could have sprung from a heart incandescent with Masonic heat

499

. Mas_onry is, in short, the highest expression of the grand idea of Fraternity, and it
is destined to he one of the most active agents in the accomplishment of that world·
wide fraternization which so especially marks the tendencies of the present age, and
whose progressive development will ultimately result in drawing in a nearer and
more perfect union all the children of the earth. It offends no prejudice, it opposes
no sect. It stands aloof from all the noisy clamors of the day. Its mission is in
secret and in silence. It" does good and communicates," but the right_ hand knows
not what the left hand docth. It is the minister to want, the angel of consolation to
patient suffering, the handmaid of religion ; for, what religion teaches from lofty
pulpits, it practically performs. Wherever there is want or sorrow, there is Masonry,
the reliever; wherever is wrong or oppression, there is Masonry, the strong arm of
support; wherever is death, or sickness, which is the shadow of death, there also
is Masonry, to bind up the wound, to close the fixed and ghastly eye, and then, with
reverent care, to commit the dead body to tile silence and retirement of tile grave.
How often have you, in this land of strange vicissitudes, been called upo~ to mini~ter to such needs as these? The strong, bold-hearted adventurer, struggling amid
discouragements and privations for his children's bread, is suddenly arrested by the
palsying hand of disease. Poverty and want environ him. A stranger in a land of
strangers, to whom shall he go for succor? The swift tides of life rush by him, and
he is cast a stranded wreck upon the shore. In the desolation and agony of his heart,
he lays down to die; no friend near that death couch-no ministering voice of consolation-no brother's hand to clasp the nerveless fingers-no upward pointing angel
of hope to guide the way to immortal life.
But stay, some one knows that poor man! Some one in all this bright world out of
which he is passing into the unknown land, must know that man! Surely, he shall not
die, and make no sign! Oh, no! He has found friends. In almost the last agonized
convulsions of his members, when !tis tongue could no longer syllable his thoughts,
he found a brother - a brother in a higher sense than the claim which our common
humanity in suffering or sore distress demands of every man-one, whose soul was
knit to that vanishing soul in all the gentle ministrations of love and charity, by ties
as strong, aye stronger, than those which knit the souls of Jonathan and David.
T4is picture, brethren, is a picture of practical Masonry, You have it framed in
all your hearts; its colors cannot fade from your memories. In your own dark hours
of desolation, the light from it will be a beacon pointing upward to Heaven!
And now, the hour for our departure has arrived. Henceforth, our paths diverge.
Prom manifold pursuits in life, and from distant homes, moved by a common impulse,
we have come up to worship near this sacred shrine, and to renew tile vows of fealty
to our common faith. I trust the hour has not been spent in vain, and that It has been
good for us to have been together. In this interchange of kindly greeting, we have
strengt.hened our fraternal ties, and in this common labor dedicated to our common
cause, we have strengthened the hands of our Craft In every land.
As Masons of California, this hour is full of deep significance. You are the representatives of the world. From distant lands and climes, from every rank and station
in life, from the most dissimilar eonditions of physical and political existence, you
have assembled on the western shore of our continent, a family of brethren bound together by a common interestaml protected by the glorious Constitution of our common
country. Yon are one, as citizens ; and owing allegiance to a common law, you share
alike in tile glory and advancement of the State. In your Masonic relations you pre·
sent the same anomaly. Of various tribes and nations, of parentages and educations
the most diverse, with wide and high partition-walls separating you one from the other,
you yet, here, to-day, meet upon common gronnd. We are all one-on earth, the
great all-embracing, loving soul of Masonry claims us as lier comm<iq children-and in
the heavens above us, the One Et\lrnal Father!

[June 25,

Special Communication of the

Before we go hence, let us review our work. Upon a solid foundation we have
placed our memorial stone. It hides from mortal eyes (we hope for ages yet to come)
in its safe and silent tomb, the records of this day. In all its appointments, and with
all the glory of its architectural design, this proud temple shall rise to its lofty roof,
a fitting and noble testimonial to the devotion of the Masonry of our State. But
there must be samething, brethren, underneath that stone, and underneath the founda·
tion which supports it, deeper than all this, or the building will not stand. The master.
builder may perform his work never so well; the apprentices and craftsmen may
labor in due subordination to the authority of the masters; the massive walls may
rise in all their solid strength to heaven; the costly jewels of our work may adorn its
various chambers; the fires may be lighted upon its inner altars ; the entrances may
be well and duly guarded ; but all, all ~ill be in vain, unless there is a deeper, surer,
and more stable foundation than that on which our corner stone reposes. What
is that nether stone? What is that upon which a true temple to Masonry must be
built? Ah, brethren, it is the deep, underlying, imperishable foundation of Masonic
love, and Masonic unity. With. that beneath the material foundation, this Temple is
indeed secure and indestructible. The solid foundations of the globe had need of no
more permanent corner stone than that structure, under whose deep bases repose
Truth, Charity, and Brotherly Love.
One prayer, one spontaneous aspiration, is a fitting conclusion to this hour: Oh
Temple ! planned with the cunning skill of laborious art, rise in all thy majesty and
beauty toward the skies! May thy walls be strength, and all thy tabernacles peace !
May the votaries who shall in the long march of centuries enter thy sacred porches,
find evermore therein repose, refreshment, peace ! May the light of thy sacred altars
burn ever like a star! May the "stranger and the sojourner in the land" ever enjoy
the blessings of thy welcome and thy shelter; and when the hour of thy decay and
dissolution crumbles thee to earth, may there be found thousands of faithful and
devoted hearts to raise thee from thy ashes with renewed splendor and more enduring
life! "So mote it be."

At the conclusion of the oration, "Old Hundred" was sung by the
choir, accompanied by the entire band, and joined in by the whole assembly; and the ceremonies were terminated with a benediction by the Grand
Chaplain.
The President, of the Hall Association, on behalf of the Masons of San
Francisco, in~ited all the brethren present from without the city, to dine
with them at the great hall in the Academy of Music, at 7t o'clock, P. M.
The procession was then re-formed, and returned to the Hall of the
Grand Lodge; where that body was called on, and, after prayer by the
Grand Chaplain and the customary music, was closed in ~mple Jj'orm.
